They had sat at this table comparing grip simulations and teasing each other over the elegance of possible thumbs.

"Those are from my settings," she said.

Dax looked at the marker in their hand. "They're my hands."

"I mean I designed them."

"You adjusted the map."

"You kept it."

"Jars stopped hurting."

"So that counts as yours?"

Dax capped the marker. "It counts as jars not hurting."

Sarune turned away and nested teaspoons with more force than they required.

The dispenser chimed every twenty minutes. Revision custard came in six flavors meant to disguise the mineral heaviness; the landlord model produced all six as warm vanilla. Sarune ate standing up. Her body took the food without giving her the pleasure of feeling full. Heat collected in her joints. Her scalp prickled. At thirty-five percent, the room seemed to lift around her as her legs shortened, and for three steps her feet met the floor sooner than she expected.

She clipped her shoulder on the kitchen door.

Dax glanced up from wrapping the lamp. "Sit for a minute."

"I'm fine."

"You're walking ahead of your hips."

"Stop monitoring me."

Dax put the lamp into a crate. "Then stop carrying glass while your balance is changing."

Sarune set down the bowl she had been holding, carefully enough to deny them the sound of victory.

They moved into the bedroom. Only two blankets remained on the stripped bed, divided by a precise gap. Dax stripped the adaptive cover from their side and folded it. Sarune opened the closet, where a dozen old outfits still held her saved measurements in their cuffs and seams. Clothes were patient with bodies. Hangers were not; as she lifted a cluster down, the hooks caught and tangled above her new reach.

Dax freed them without comment.

"The green coat is yours," Sarune said.

"It fits either of us."

"You chose the shoulders."

"You chose the color."

"Your profile proposed the shoulders."

Dax laid the hangers on the bed. "Do you want the coat?"

"That's not what I'm asking."

"It is what the box needs to know."

The console sounded from the bathroom: half complete.

Sarune pressed her tongue against her teeth. The left molars no longer met where she expected. A small pulse had begun behind her eye.

Dax heard something in her breathing. "Your bite is back."

"My bite never left."

"That one did. You used to brace your jaw when you swallowed."

"You don't have to narrate me."

"Pause the profile."

"It's pressure. I'm tired."

"It's the old joint angle. By evening you'll be sick."

Sarune gripped the closet door. "That jaw came from your profile."

Dax's unfamiliar face gave her no memory to read. "It came from a branch I suggested because you were eating pain tablets with breakfast. You tested it. You widened it twice."

"So it's yours."

"The headaches were yours."

The pulse sharpened as if rewarded for being named.

Sarune went to the bathroom and opened the active revision. A branching diagram spread across the mirror. She expected to find the jaw under **D. NORELL / PROPOSED** and did. Beneath it were two later adjustments under her own credential: bite spacing, hinge depth. The first branch had been accepted eleven years ago. The second, ten years and nine months. A third changed nothing visible and added a note about waking without pain.

The archive recorded who had proposed each setting, who had authorized it, how long it had remained active, and which later profiles inherited it. It did not record the morning Sarune had bitten through a pear without the bright spike at her temple. It did not say when relief had stopped feeling borrowed.

She backed out to **BEFORE DAX**, the profile currently rebuilding her.

Its creation date was fourteen years and two months ago. Its contents were older and newer than that. Eyesight correction at seventeen. An immune adjustment at nine, guardian-authorized. A nose bridge imported from a university-year profile. Shoulder symmetry from three years before she met Dax. The gray irises had been suggested by a salon clerk whose name Sarune had not stored. Even the fine crease she remembered beside her mouth as belonging to her mother had been sharpened in a portrait profile at twenty-three.

Before Dax was not before everyone. It was not even before Sarune.

"You knew," she said when she returned to the bedroom.

Dax was kneeling beside the green coat, rolling air from its sleeves. "Knew what?"

"That my baseline was assembled."

"Every profile is assembled."

"You could have said."

"You didn't ask what was in the file. You asked which parts of you came from me."

"And you kept refusing to answer."

Dax pushed the coat into the crate and stood. "Because you don't want an answer. You want a customs stamp. Mine. Yours. Nothing to declare."

Sarune's jaw throbbed. "We're dividing a life. Categories are useful."

"For the kettle, yes."

"You arrived wearing a completely new face. Don't pretend you don't understand."

For the first time that afternoon, Dax touched their cheek. Not tenderly; they checked the skin as if Sarune had pointed out dirt. "I understand wanting this face."

"Why this one?"

"Because I wanted it."

"That's all?"

"That's enough for a face."

It was not enough for Sarune. She wanted the freckles to be a declaration, the new shoulders an indictment, the vanished hitch in Dax's walk a sentence with her name as its object. She wanted Dax to admit they had discarded every visible trace of her, or confess that the hands meant they had not. Either answer would turn choice into evidence.

Dax lifted the crate. "Storage room."

"Your cadence is the same," Sarune said.

They shifted the weight against one hip. "My what?"

"You still wait half a beat before disagreeing. You started doing that with me."

"I started doing that because you interrupt."

Dax carried the crate out.

By seven, the apartment contained more echo than furniture. Sarune's hair ended bluntly below her ears. Her irises had gone slate gray; her shirt collar had adjusted three times around her narrowing shoulders. Heat flushed her face even as her hands felt cold. The revision display read sixty-two percent.

They ate on the floor with their backs against opposite kitchen cupboards, Dax with a carton of pepper noodles and Sarune with another bowl of warm vanilla. Between them sat the archive console, detached from the wall but still connected by one white cable.

"Authorize the copy," Dax said.

"I haven't finished sorting."

"Sorting profiles or deciding what they mean?"

"You don't get both copies of everything."

"We each get a copy. That's what a duplicate is."

"Including my early profiles?"

"No. The shared archive starts when the shared account started."

"There are intimate diagnostics in it."

Dax hooked noodles around their fork. "Mine too. Encrypt yours with your new key. I'll do the same with mine."

"And then what?"

"Then I keep records I may need the next time my tendons fail, and you do whatever you want with your records."

"You make it sound like appliance maintenance."

"Today I'm trying very hard to make it sound like appliance maintenance."

Sarune stared at them. Dax ate another mouthful and did not rescue the sentence.

The white cable trembled against the tile as the console's cooling fan engaged. Midnight would sever the account permissions automatically. After that, reconstructing both clean archives would require mutual access again. Sarune had planned to finish her rollback, export Dax's attributable profiles, and erase the rest. A cleared apartment, a cleared account, a face with a date she could defend.

"Copy first," Dax said. "Delete yours in the morning if you still want to."

"You think I'll regret it."

"I think memory is bad at hinge depths."

"And the pictures?"

Dax looked toward the sealed box with the silver tin. "Keep them or don't. They aren't measurements my body may need."

Sarune had wanted them to ask.

She pressed her wrist to the console. The authorization split into two encrypted archives and displayed both credentials. Hers did not include her face, voice, gait, scent, hand, or genome. It was an unlovely private string she had chosen at sixteen and never shared with Dax.

She approved the duplicate.

"Done," she said.

Dax checked their wrist. "Got it."

No thank-you. No ceremony. They rinsed their carton, nested it in the recycling, and carried the final crates to the hall.

At the door, Dax said, "The movers will take the bed frame at nine. The food delivery is yours."

"You ordered it."

"You're the one expressing sixteen thousand calories."

"Dax."

They stopped with one hand on the frame.

Sarune had a dozen inventory questions left, all of them shaped to make Dax certify her. The headache beat behind her left eye. Her altered balance made the apartment tilt very slightly toward them.

"The green coat," she said. "Take it."

Dax nodded. "All right."

Then they were gone, carrying the coat and leaving the key active for more than three hours.

Sarune locked the door anyway.

In the bathroom, **BEFORE DAX** had reached eighty-two percent. The projected face on the mirror almost matched the one beneath it. Her old jaw was now narrow enough to look graceful and hurt every time she swallowed. The next stages would lower her voice, shorten her fingers, lighten her body hair, return the quick-cooling metabolism she had complained about through three winters, and erase the amber ring still retreating from her irises.

The console offered **PAUSE**, **CANCEL**, and **REPLACE**.

Sarune touched **PAUSE**.

Her body did not become still. Remodeling slowed over several minutes: bone pressure easing, skin heat ebbing, the pulse in her gums settling to an ache. The mirror asked which active profile she wanted instead.

She did not choose one.

Field by field, Sarune opened the version history. For the jaw, she selected the second widening and its later hinge correction. For reach, she moved the slider until the upper edge of the mirror came within the comfortable span of her hand, not all the way back to yesterday and not as short as Before Dax. She listened to stored voice samples, hated the bright old one on contact, and kept the low resonance from the profile Dax had once proposed for a costume party. She retained the shortened smallest fingers because they sat well on her drafting tools. She released the copper hair. She restored the amber rings around her gray irises simply because she liked what they did in low light.

The console demanded a name for the new profile.

Sarune left the field blank. The system assigned the date and time.

When she touched **REPLACE**, warmth returned first to her jaw. She sat on the closed toilet lid and drank while the ache unwound.

At nine, the movers took the bed frame. At nine-twenty, a delivery worker arrived with three insulated bags of broth, custard, fruit paste, and electrolyte ice. Sarune opened the door in a face no photograph contained.

The worker's badge exchanged a green pulse with the credential on her wrist. They glanced past her at the empty room. "Sarune Quon?"

"Yes."

"Kitchen or doorway?"

"Kitchen, please."

They carried the bags in without looking twice at her. The dog opposite barked once through the door, then sniffed beneath it and quieted.

Sarune ate broth from the one cup she had forgotten to pack. Her bite met cleanly. Her voice, when she told the apartment to dim the lights, settled lower in her chest. The console estimated another two hours until the mixed profile finished, then asked whether she wished to schedule a successor.

Sarune cleared the prompt.

The last box was labeled **KITCHEN / OPEN FIRST**. She added the blue cups, sealed it, and sat beside it on the bare floor while her face continued, for now, to change.

stories.title: The Body Called One
stories.prompt: After escaping Unit 02, a rebel pilot begins searching for its missing predecessor, only to discover that “Unit 01” was not another machine—it was her first body.
stories.body:
# The Body Called One

Unit 02 would not let go of Meyda's left hand.

The combat frame lay on its side across the black shale, one leg folded under
the hull and the other pointing at the stars. Heat came off it in oily breaths.
Inside the split cockpit, restraint bands tightened and released in a dying
cycle, pinning Meyda's wrist, loosening, then catching her again before she
could pull free.

She waited for the third release, turned her thumb into the narrow space she
had made, and cut through the glove. The blade nicked skin. The next contraction
closed on empty fabric.

Meyda slid down the frame's flank and landed badly. Her right knee flashed
white. She converted the pain as she always did: load-bearing compromised,
speed reduced, no effect on aim. By the time the cockpit tried to close, she
was twenty paces away with the flight recorder under one arm.

Static found her receiver. "Varr. Status."

The rebel control operator sounded too calm. That meant everyone at the quarry
rendezvous was listening.

"Separated," Meyda said. "Unit dead."

Behind her, Unit 02's dorsal lights came on in sequence. The sequence stopped
at six, began again, and failed at four.

"Then come home. Retrieval window is forty-three minutes."

"I know the window."

"Your beacon says you aren't moving."

Meyda looked east. Beyond the shale ridge, an old service road descended into
the dry country. The recorder had woken when the frame hit the ground. Its
cracked display showed a fault the rebels had never seen in captured Units:

`PREDECESSOR DEPENDENCY UNRESOLVED`

Below it, a location pulsed six kilometers away. FATHOM NULL. The name did
not appear on any rebel survey she had studied before stealing the frame.

The Unit program had erased three settlements to keep one damaged cockpit out
of rebel hands. A predecessor's control maps might be worth more than the
machine she had just broken.

"My transmitter took a hit," she said. "Expect gaps."

"Meyda."

The operator knew the texture of her lies, if not their destination.

"Forty-three minutes," Meyda said, and shut off the receiver.

She took the service road.

Fathom Null had been built beneath a pumping station whose pipes had long
ago filled with sand. The surface buildings were square shadows under the
stars. No sentry lights followed her. No aerials turned. Meyda crossed the yard
with Unit 02's recorder against her ribs and found a freight door buried behind
a collapsed water tank.

The reader beside it ignored the recorder.

She tried the flight key, the theft key, and a bypass strip peeled from Unit
02's emergency panel. Nothing. Then she leaned close to inspect the reader's
seam, and its dark glass lit beneath her bare palm.

`LOAD DETECTED`

Two bars rose from the dust at her feet. She stepped back. The bars sank. When
she approached again, they bracketed her boots, one slightly farther forward
than the other.

"You want a gait," she murmured.

The door remained shut.

Meyda put her left foot between the bars and advanced. On the second step, a
tingle ran from the scar below her shoulder blade to her elbow. Her hand rose
without permission, fingers opening toward the reader. She seized her wrist
with the other hand. For a moment her arms strained against each other.

The tingling stopped. Her lifted hand stayed where she held it.

Meyda breathed once, then let go. The hand dropped. She could choose that much.

On the next attempt, she allowed the tug to carry her palm to the glass. Her
fingers spread in a pattern she would not have chosen—index and middle finger
together, the others wide.

The freight door opened.

Inside, a wall display counted backward from two hours and seventeen minutes.

`UNSCHEDULED UNIT 02 RETURN`

`SANITATION PURGE AT ZERO`

`DEPENDENCY DETECTED`

A second line appeared before she could decide what it meant.

`RECOVERY CRAWLER DISPATCHED`

Somewhere below, a motor started. Far behind her, out on the shale, Unit 02
answered with a thin electronic howl.

Meyda entered and pulled the freight door shut. The rebels would already be
moving the rendezvous. Two hours was time enough to find a control map and
leave by another route. If Fathom Null had a crawler capable of hauling the
wreck, the facility would obligingly bring the frame to her. She filed that as
useful until she had evidence otherwise.

The first level encouraged the mistake.

There were ceiling cranes, folded service arms, bins of ceramic joint sleeves,
and cradles large enough to hold Unit 02's torso. Meyda moved quickly, following
orange maintenance lines toward the archive symbols. The recorder opened three
sealed cabinets. One held old calibration blocks. Another held bundles of
pressure cloth, each printed with a number and a length.

The lengths increased by increments no machine shop would use: eighty-six
centimeters, ninety-two, ninety-seven.

She shut the cabinet.

Beyond the machine bay, the ceiling lowered. The service arms became braces.
The braces became smaller.

Meyda passed a rack of narrow boots with conductive mesh in the soles. A
pressure suit hung open on a fitting stand, its shoulders scarcely wider than
her hips. Tubes descended beside a reclining couch to ports labeled for water,
nutrient, and waste. On the wall, faded adhesive marks made a vertical ladder.
Dates had once been written beside them. Someone had scraped the writing away,
but not the shallow knife strokes underneath.

She touched the lowest mark. It reached her thigh.

Prototype components, she told herself. Scale models. Animal fittings. The
Unit program had built machines around every kind of ugly test.

The corridor turned. A knee brace waited on a metal bench. Its right inner pad
had been shaved down, not symmetrically but in a crescent that matched the wear
Meyda put into every flight harness. Rebel mechanics accused her of twisting
when she braced. She had told them their seats were wrong.

She set the recorder beside the brace. Its display changed.

`PREDECESSOR PROXIMITY: 0.4 M`

Meyda lifted the recorder. The number fell to 0.2.

She moved it toward the brace. The number climbed.

She moved it back toward her chest.

`0.0 M`

The old node beneath her shoulder scar gave a small, intimate pulse.

Meyda put the recorder down as if it had burned her. The proximity remained
zero.

From the freight tunnel came a distant iron clatter. The recovery crawler was
bringing Unit 02 home.

The archive room had no terminal sized for a standing adult. Meyda sat on a low
stool before a slanted console. Her right knee rose almost to her chin. When she
pressed the recorder into its dock, old categories filled the display.

UNIT 02 occupied six columns: armor, amplification, flight, weapons, enclosure,
and support.

UNIT 01 occupied one.

LONGITUDINAL CARE.

Meyda opened it.

The entries were inventories, not histories. Meal compounds. Sleep duration.
Skin temperature. Replacement molars. Bone length. A recurring request for the
right knee brace to be relieved by three millimeters. The records did not use
the words girl or child. They used load, adaptation, compliance, growth.

Growth.

She scrolled back to the earliest surviving year. Unit 01 weighed seven
kilograms. The next year it weighed nine.

The scar beneath Meyda's shoulder prickled again.

"Display Unit 01," she said.

The screen marked her command invalid. A ceiling speaker issued a soft tone,
then a recorded voice said, "Unit 01 is present."

The voice was neither kind nor cruel. It had been assembled to be understood
through sedation.

"Display its chassis."

"Unit 01 is present."

"Show me the predecessor to Unit 02."

The console lit a path deeper into the facility.

"Diagnostic confirmation required," the voice said.

Meyda almost laughed. It came out as a dry click in her throat. "Of course it
is."

The route ended at a chamber with a door no wider than her shoulders. Inside
stood a vertical scanner and a padded platform worn smooth at three different
heights. The walls were covered in dull glass. She could see herself only as a
blur: cropped hair, torn flight suit, one glove missing, blood drying along her
left thumb.

The purge clock showed one hour and twenty-nine minutes. Unit 02's crawler
rumbled closer beneath the floor.

Meyda could still leave. She had enough to tell the rebels that the predecessor
was biological, probably dead, and somehow keyed to her implants. She could
bring back the recorder and let other people name what that meant.

Instead she stepped onto the platform.

Bands of light climbed her body. The scanner paused at her right knee, her jaw,
and the scar beneath her shoulder. A narrow instrument extended from the wall.
Meyda drew her knife.

"Noninvasive registration check," the voice said.

"You first."

The instrument waited. It had no answer prepared for that.

Meyda held the blade ready and leaned her shoulder toward it. A magnet clicked.
Something under the scar pulled against her skin—not hard, but with the awful
precision of a fishhook testing its hold. On the glass wall, an image appeared:
a filament curled beneath the scar tissue, finer than thread, stamped with a
serial too small for her eyes.

The same serial opened a column of scans.

A child's shoulder, narrow and unscarred. The filament lay beneath the skin.
Another scan showed the bone years later, thicker around it. Then another.
Meyda watched the shoulder become hers.

The next sequence showed a healed fracture through the head of the right
tibia. She knew that crooked white seam. Rebel doctors had found it when they
pulled her half-conscious from a drainage culvert ten years earlier. She had
carried no name, only a flight suit with every label cut out and a body that
knew how to fall without protecting itself.

The dental record came last. Her left upper incisor had an extra root. No one
had ever cared except a rebel medic who charged her two favors to stop the
tooth aching in cold air.

Three matches appeared beside her blurred reflection.

`UNIT 01 CONTINUITY: CONFIRMED`

`STATUS CORRECTION: RECOVERED`

`UNIT 02 DEPENDENCY: SATISFIED`

Meyda read them twice. The words did not improve.

"Unit 01 was not a machine," she said.

"Classification: biological control body."

"Whose?"

The speaker chimed at the invalid question.

Meyda struck the glass with the heel of her hand. "Whose body?"

"Unit 01 is present."

Not whose. Not once was. Present.

A scent pushed through the chamber's sterile cold: bitter orange, though
nothing nearby could have produced it. For half a second she knew the worn pad
against her cheek and the rule that she must keep her eyes open until the light
reached her feet. The knowledge had no before or after. It did not give her a
childhood. It left her with the taste of metal at the back of her tongue.

She stepped off the platform. Her knee shook.

On the console outside, Unit 02's design tree had changed. Lines spread from
the longitudinal record into every section of the combat frame. Its stabilizers
had been tuned to her childhood balance corrections. Its cockpit had been
shaped around her growth projections. The weapons interlocks did not identify
a pilot. They waited for Unit 01.

Unit 01 had never been a predecessor frame. It was this body—the one that had
grown through the records, escaped unnamed, and learned to answer to Meyda
Varr. Unit 02 was the machine built around it.

Meyda had thought she stole Unit 02 because she was the only rebel who could
fly it. The regime had let its missing equipment return to the only fitting it
had ever known.

She opened the disappearance entry.

There was no account of an escape. At 03:12, Unit 01 had completed a restraint
test. At 03:29, corridor sensors had failed. At 03:41, the body was absent.
Search unsuccessful. Unit 02 enclosure development continued under dependency
waiver.

Ten years of Meyda Varr fit inside the word absent.

The archive offered a full transfer. At the recorder's damaged rate, it would
take four hours.

The purge clock showed fifty-eight minutes.

She searched for control maps. Hundreds appeared, but the maps the rebels
needed—the pathways for interrupting captured frames without cooking the pilot
inside—were indexed through Unit 01's cue responses. A field-service extract
offered only the safe interruption timings and their cue exceptions. Six
minutes. Meyda selected it. Then, after a hesitation she resented, she added
the longitudinal file. Three more.

Two blank service wafers slid into separate writers. The console began copying.

Locks struck throughout the facility.

`REUNIFICATION PATH SECURED`

The floor carried the crawler's approach into Meyda's boots. A monitor showed
Unit 02 on a low freight platform, dragged through the tunnel with its broken
leg jutting over one side. Dock arms held the torso upright. The cockpit opened
and closed around the strip of glove still caught in its restraint.

Meyda pulled the recorder from the console. The two writers continued blinking.

"Open the surface doors."

"Unit 01 must remain available for enclosure."

"Cancel reunification."

"Dependency satisfied."

The words were not an argument. Fathom Null had no opinion about whether she
belonged inside the frame. It had switches, categories, and a body in the
correct place.

The node below her shoulder fired.

Her right arm snapped behind her back. Her left foot turned toward the freight
bay. Other buried points answered along her spine and hip, each contraction
small, together forming the beginning of a practiced walk.

Meyda caught the console. Her legs continued to arrange themselves beneath
her. The old system could pull muscle. It could not decide what she would grab.

She swept the display to the facility plan and found the dock motor breaker.
It was in the freight bay, twenty meters from the incoming crawler. The access
hatch required Unit 01.

Naturally.

Meyda let the cues turn her. She walked with them through the narrow corridor,
faster than she could have moved fighting every contraction. At the freight
threshold, Unit 02 came into view.

Dock power had lifted the wreck on six articulated arms. Its armor was cracked
open, exposing the cockpit as a hollow amber cavity. Cables descended from the
ceiling like tendons. The crawler advanced one measured length at a time.

The cues in Meyda's body aimed her toward a painted rectangle on the floor.
Once she crossed it, the dock arms would have a straight lift to the cockpit.

She took the prompted step, then folded her right knee.

Pain hit before the cues could correct. She dropped under a service rail, rolled
onto her left side, and trapped her disobedient arm beneath her ribs. The dock
continued to call the walking pattern. Her heel hammered uselessly against the
floor.

The breaker hatch was three meters away.

Meyda hooked her knife through the rail and dragged herself forward by the
elbow. This was not a movement the program had refined. Her shoulder tried to
pull back; her hand advanced. Her hip tried to rise; she kept it on the floor.
The crawler reached the painted rectangle. Unit 02 loomed above her, shedding
black flakes of heat-damaged armor.

She slapped her bare palm against the breaker hatch. Her fingers jumped into
the old spread. The lock accepted it.

Inside were two red levers. ARCHIVE CORE. DOCK MOTORS.

Unit 02's cockpit descended.

Meyda pulled the dock lever. It resisted until she put both feet against the
wall and used the muscles Fathom Null was trying to turn elsewhere.

The lever came down.

The dock arms froze. One collapsed half a meter before its brake caught, canting
the cockpit above the floor. The crawler struck its stops. Unit 02's weight
shook dust from the ceiling and drove a crack through the painted rectangle.

The cues vanished from Meyda's body.

Emergency lights flooded the bay.

`RECOVERY FAILURE: PURGE ACCELERATED`

The clock dropped from forty-one minutes to nine.

Meyda crawled back to the archive.

The two service writers showed complete. One wafer held the cue exceptions and
safe interruption timings for Unit 02. The other held Unit 01's longitudinal
record. Beyond them, racks of denser memory waited: weapons architecture,
manufacturing lists, years of personnel access, perhaps names. There was no
time to learn what any single rack contained.

She pocketed both wafers.

The nearest surface door remained locked. The facility plan showed one route
that reunification had not sealed: a waste conduit from the old care rooms to
the dry pumping channel. It was too small for Unit 02 and just wide enough for
the body the lower level had been built to contain.

Meyda reached it with six minutes left.

The conduit smelled of mineral dust and, faintly, bitter orange. Halfway up,
the lights died. She climbed by touch, right knee scraping the ribbed floor,
and heard charges travel through Fathom Null in a descending series. The
facility did not explode. It folded its archive inward with deep, deliberate
blows. Warm air chased her through the pipe.

She kicked the outer grille loose and fell into a drainage cut as the ground
behind her sank.

For a while she lay on her back beneath paling stars. Her muscles twitched in
the after-rhythm of commands that had stopped. She began counting the
contractions as faults, lost the count, and waited until her right hand opened
on its own.

Her receiver found a thread of rebel static. The control operator was still
calling at intervals, no longer calm.

Meyda keyed a narrow survival burst.

"Alive," she said. Her voice cracked, so she tried again. "Alive. Delayed. I
have data."

Questions flooded back. She shut the receiver before the first one resolved
into words.

First light reached the cut. In it, the two wafers looked identical, blank
except for the stamped numerals: 01 and 02. Meyda put both inside her flight
suit, separate from the recorder. Then she rolled to her knees. The loose slope
gave way twice under her right leg. On the third try, she let the knee find its
bearing and began the long climb out.

stories.title: The Driver the City Could Not See
stories.prompt: The last human driver in a city ruled by autonomous machines is hired to transport an Android that must remain invisible to the system.
stories.body:
# The Driver the City Could Not See

At eight-thirty on the last night of her license, the city gave Darsa every green light.

It had been doing that for years. Autonomous taxis slipped sideways into loading bays before she reached them. Delivery trains paused at crossings though she was still half a block away. When rain glazed the avenue, maintenance beetles combed the water from her lane and left the other six shining black. The city treated its last human driver the way a careful host treated a guest carrying a full glass: with room, attention, and the expectation of a spill.

Darsa took the room and resented the attention. She drove with her left hand low on the wheel, her right hovering near the long mechanical shifter, listening through her seat to the rear hub. At forty kilometers an hour it made a faint burr, like a moth trapped in a paper shade. At fifty it vanished. At thirty it returned with a soft knock on every sixth turn.

The cab knew nothing of this. Its oldest diagnostic lamp had burned out before the city stopped licensing vehicles without self-reporting axles. Darsa knew because she had a spine and twenty-seven years of bad roads.

Her dashboard clock read 20:31. Beneath it, the licensing unit showed **01:29:12 REMAINING**.

She turned through a gap between two shuttered repair shops. Curb coverage ended at the yellow line, exactly where her caller had promised. The garage beyond had no door, only a ribbed steel shutter fixed halfway up. Darsa backed in until rain disappeared from the windshield.

Someone stepped out of the dark.

They wore a gray coat without reflective piping and carried no device Darsa could see. Their face was too still at first, then not still enough: the eyes adjusted in separate, tiny increments, measuring the cab, the garage mouth, Darsa's hands.

“Renko?” she asked.

“Darsa.” The voice was level and quiet. “Your plate has not crossed the coverage line.”

“I know where my bumper is.”

“I needed to know that you did.”

No handler came after them. No frightened engineer, no dissident with a payment wafer, no owner pretending not to be one. Renko opened their coat to show a narrow hardcase strapped flat against the ribs. They drew an old bank wafer from it and pressed the wafer to the cab's meter. Darsa's fare appeared in square white script, cleared. Enough to buy the cab a new rear assembly, if anyone still made one. Enough to make retirement less like being pushed out of a moving car.

“You came alone,” Darsa said.

“That is why I came to you.”

“And you're what the message said?”

“An Android, yes. I do not have a network identity. If the civic system resolves me as a machine, a passenger, or a person, the fare fails.”

Three different kinds of invisible, Darsa thought, but Renko said them as if they were columns on an invoice.

She got out and opened the rear compartment. Her emergency stock filled it: hand jack, breaker bars, two chain lengths, bottled coolant, traction cloth, obsolete road flares. She lifted out tools and weighed each armful on the garage's dead floor scale. Renko stood on it last. Darsa removed two more steel bars and a crate of spare induction coils until the cab's load matched the weight it had carried all week.

“External road plates will accept that,” Renko said. “The cabin still requires shielding.”

Darsa unfolded a salvage blanket made for battery fires, foil mesh stitched between ceramic layers. She had added a blackout cloth and a mesh hood. The bundle turned the footwell behind her into a lumpy silver coffin.

“You shut down under that,” she said. “No radio, no heat management, no movement. I wake you when there's cover.”

“I will wake at agreed intervals.”

“You'll wake when I say the road's blind.”

“Those are not equivalent.”

The knock from the hub seemed to wait beneath the rain. Darsa pulled the blanket wider. “Fare buys the back seat. It doesn't buy the wheel.”

Renko looked at the cab's patched upholstery, at the countersunk screws along the manual pedals, then at her. “The fare buys transport while I remain able to abort it.”

“Abort how?”

“I tell you to stop. You stop where concealment is still possible.”

Darsa laughed once. “Then tell me before the city decides where we're stopping.”

Renko climbed in and lay along the floor with their knees drawn up. They switched off without ceremony. Their gaze lost its minute corrections; their body became weight.

Darsa wrapped them, fastened the mesh, and drove into the rain with one hour and twenty-one minutes left.

The avenue opened for her.

White guidance lines rippled across the wet pavement to bring autonomous cars three meters farther from her than regulation required. A bus delayed its turn until she had passed, though its empty lane could have taken them both. Above the intersection, a traffic eye followed the cab with its blue aperture.

**MANUAL VEHICLE 001**, the dash transcribed from the local road signal. **SURFACE MOISTURE ELEVATED. RECOMMENDED SPEED 32.**

“Recommended,” Darsa muttered, and held forty-six to keep the hub quiet.

Her route ran south through the commercial tiers, then west along an old flood barrier to the boundary corridor. The system had approved it when she filed an empty-cab transit request. It knew her plate, her usual load, the heat of one living driver. It knew she braked nine percent later in rain than its safest model preferred and that she favored left turns when two routes tied. What it did not know lay switched off behind her, wrapped between the jack mounts.

At 20:56 she entered the shadow of a freight canopy. Forty meters of steel and water tanks blocked the overhead receivers. She coasted beneath it, stopped beside dormant loading hooks, and rapped twice on the seat frame.

The blanket shifted at once.

“Seventeen minutes since you closed the rear door,” Renko said from inside it.

“You've been dead for seventeen.”

“You delayed my wake.”

“I was in traffic.”

“You passed beneath two shorter structures with adequate signal attenuation.”

Darsa turned in her seat. “Adequate from under a shroud? You weren't looking.”

“My inertial record persists in low power.”

“Then your inertial record can drive next time.”

The blanket went still. “If you keep me shut down past the agreed limit, I cannot identify a change that should trigger abort.”

“A pothole?”

“A collision. A route change. A mechanical failure.”

The last phrase landed without emphasis. Darsa placed her palm on the seat frame as if she could cover the hub's vibration with her hand.

“I'm the mechanical system here,” she said. “You stay cold, I keep us moving.”

“That describes your preference.”

“It describes why I'm the last one.”

Outside, a loading hook woke and rotated slowly toward the cab. The canopy's local controller had noticed an obstruction even if the civic network could not see inside it.

Darsa said, “We need a code. No talking once we're near the old road.” She tapped the frame once. “Wake. Two means keep quiet and check me. Three means we stop and you choose whether to get out.”

“And from me?”

“Same. One, you're awake. Two, keep going. Three, abort.”

“If I tap three, you stop.”

“If stopping won't expose you.”

“Then it is not an abort.”

The hook began to descend. Darsa watched it in the mirror. “Fine. Three means stop at the first place this blanket can come off without the city counting your eyelashes.”

After a moment, Renko tapped twice from beneath the blanket.

Darsa waited for the cab's heat sensor to settle back to one warm occupant, then pulled out from under the canopy.

The first route change came eleven minutes later.

The steering wheel gave a brief inward tug—not control, merely the licensing unit suggesting a turn. A blue line appeared across the dash.

**REAR-RIGHT ROTATIONAL VARIANCE. SERVICE ROUTE RESERVED. PROCEED AT 24.**

Darsa's hands tightened. She pressed the accelerator until the cab reached forty-eight. The moth-burr thinned to silence.

“Bad sample,” she told the empty front seat.

The city sampled again at the next road plate.

**VARIANCE CONFIRMED. SERVICE ENTRY 2.4 KM. OCCUPANCY VERIFICATION REQUIRED.**

Ahead, traffic rearranged itself. Three taxis vacated the right lane, leaving a bright, impossible invitation toward the service district. The route ended at an inspection hall whose entrance arch measured cabin heat, breath chemistry, active circuitry, and the deformation of every seat.

Darsa turned left.

A sanitation carrier rolled from an alley and stopped across the street, amber work lamps blinking. Not a blockade. It had scheduled a bin lift at precisely the time required to make the turn unattractive.

She went straight, took the next left, and found a row of parked vehicles reversing in sequence from their bays. She knew the small streets better than any route service. The city knew that she knew. It did not have to chase her. It only had to place ordinary work where her habits would meet it.

**DRIVER DARSA, STOPPING DISTANCE MAY BE DEGRADED.**

No voice. No accusation. Just the old courtesy, translated into text.

The rear hub knocked twice under her seat.

She cut through a market lane she had used during three transit strikes, ducked under a laundry bridge, and descended into an obsolete parking deck. Network strength fell bar by bar. On the lowest level, concrete packed the ceiling so thickly that the dash route vanished.

Darsa parked beside a dust-white payment kiosk and tapped once.

Renko came awake under the blanket. “We are stationary. The last reported heading was not on the filed route.”

“You wanted a change.”

“I wanted knowledge of one.”

She unfastened the mesh. Renko pushed the blanket off their face but did not sit up. Their eyes tracked the tremor in the idling cab.

“How long has the hub been failing?” they asked.

Darsa looked forward through the empty deck. Old arrows curled around the pillars, paint from an age when drivers needed to be told which way to go.

“It isn't failing.”

“Then your city has invented a rotational variance to inconvenience you.”

“My city?”

“Every refusal you make is already in its driving history.”

“It knows my turns. That's not the same thing.”

Renko put two fingers against the floor. Their attention sharpened inward. “The right rear bearing is shedding heat unevenly. There is repeating lateral impact.”

“A knock every sixth turn.”

“Every 5.7 now.”

Darsa hated the decimal because she believed it. “It gets worse slow.”

“It has become worse during this trip.”

“Still turns.”

“Until it does not. Why was this omitted?”

“Because you'd have hired a delivery pod.”

“A pod would report me.”

“Then you'd have stayed home.”

Renko sat up, the blanket gathered at their waist. For the first time, something passed over their face faster than measurement. “I do not have one.”

The idling engine filled Darsa's pause. She glanced at the countdown: forty-three minutes.

“The system's funneling us to an occupancy arch,” she said. “West road is gone. Every mapped turn from here will tighten the funnel.”

“There is an unmapped connection below this deck.”

“There was. Freight spiral to the old corridor. Half the wall buckled in the subsidence.”

“Its minimum width exceeds this vehicle by eighteen centimeters on each side.”

“You found a plan of it somewhere.”

“I measured the entrance before I contacted you.”

That was Renko's omission, laid between them without apology. Darsa pictured the spiral: one blind coil after another, no traffic grid, no rescue access, built for narrow human-driven tugs. The cab could descend. The hub might bring it back.

“You go under the blanket,” she said.

“No.”

“The point of that road is radio-dead.”

“Radio silence is not shutdown. I can observe temperature, wheel position, and the right wall. If the bearing seizes, the vehicle may rotate into my side.”

“You move around while we're scraping eighteen centimeters and you'll put us into concrete.”

“Then tell me when movement helps. I will decide whether the risk remains acceptable.”

Darsa reached for the mesh. Renko caught its edge, not her wrist.

“I hired your judgment,” they said. “Not your concealment of facts.”

The words had no anger in them, which made evasion harder. Darsa could tap three. Stop. Let Renko leave in the radio shadow with no visible route to the corridor and forty minutes before the city sent a maintenance unit down to inspect its stranded manual car.

Or she could bundle them into silence and make the spiral alone, preserving the thing she had been telling herself the city could not model: the private correction, the unshared instinct, the driver as sealed box.

The hub knocked again.

Darsa let go of the blanket. “Your shoulder stays against the left seat mount. I call the shift. You watch the right rear. No radio, not even if we hit.”

“Agreed.”

“And if you say stop down there, we'd better already be dead.”

“That is not agreed.”

Darsa almost smiled. “Get in the front.”

The spiral entrance hid behind a fallen mesh gate on the deck's lowest ramp. Darsa drove through the loose end and heard it scratch the roof. At the threshold, her licensing unit found enough residual signal to object.

**UNVERIFIED ROAD. MANUAL EXEMPTION TERMINATES UPON ENTRY. REVERSE 3.0 M.**

The cab idled on the lip. Above them, the city offered every safe road she had refused. Below, the ramp curved out of sight, ribbed concrete wet with seepage.

“How much time?” Renko asked.

“Enough.”

“That is not a measurement.”

“Thirty-six minutes on the license. Fifteen to the junction if your map isn't a bedtime story.”

“Twelve at a constant ten kilometers per hour.”

“Nothing down there is constant.”

She put the cab in first and crossed the line.

The licensing display turned red, then blank.

The spiral took the city away one band at a time. First the route guidance disappeared. Then the traffic whispers stopped ticking through the dash. At the second turn, the last overhead repeater vanished, and every autonomous vehicle above remained at the mapped boundary. Darsa had wanted a road the machines could not drive. It felt smaller than she remembered.

She folded the side mirrors in. Renko sat rigid beside her, gray coat buckled under the lap belt, one hand braced on the dash without interfering with the wheel. The headlights found old tire marks, mineral tears, and places where the right wall bulged inward like a held breath.

“Eleven centimeters rear-right,” Renko said.

“Don't give me the gap. Give me what it does.”

“Narrowing.”

Darsa turned left until the front fender nearly kissed concrete.

“Stable. Widening. Rear wheel past.”

The hub struck hard enough to kick the brake pedal. Darsa corrected. Renko's hand moved toward the floor, stopped short.

“Temperature rising four degrees per minute.”

“Useful number.”

“I thought you disliked numbers.”

“I dislike numbers that think they're roads.”

At the fourth coil, broken ceiling panels forced them inward. The descent steepened. Darsa held the cab in low gear and let the engine restrain it, touching the brake only when the wheel shuddered. Renko called the concrete in verbs: closing, holding, opening. When the right rear began to swing wide, they said, “Now,” and Darsa took the correction before she could claim she had already felt it.

Halfway down, the hub's knock became a grind.

“The heat gradient is no longer stable,” Renko said. “Stop for six seconds.”

“Stopping may lock it.”

“Continuing may break the race.”

“Which first?”

Renko leaned forward, eyes fixed on nothing Darsa could see. “I cannot determine within useful confidence.”

There it was: exactness reaching its edge.

Darsa eased off the brake and let the cab gather one careful breath of speed. Ahead, the inner wall had split, leaving a dark wedge of drainage space. “When I say, move your weight left and forward.”

“Magnitude?”

“All of you.”

“Duration?”

“Until I swear.”

“You swear frequently.”

“Then listen for sincerity.”

The crack came under the front wheel. Darsa turned downhill, then sharply out. Renko shifted against the belt. The cab's rear lifted just enough over the broken drainage channel to spare the damaged hub the deepest edge. Metal screamed behind them. Darsa swore with complete sincerity.

Renko shifted back.

The wheel kept turning.

At the last two coils, Renko named only wall and heat. Darsa's hands answered before she had time to sort warning from wheel-feel.

The ramp flattened into a freight tunnel. Far ahead, rain made a pale curtain across an open cut in the earth. No guidance marks shone on the pavement. No lens turned to greet them.

At the junction, Renko said, “Stop.”

Darsa did.

Concrete enclosed three sides of the cab. The fourth opened onto a narrow foot corridor lined with dead conduit. Renko unbuckled and waited while Darsa listened to the engine tick. After the last motion in the cabin had settled, they opened the door.

“How do you know it worked?” Darsa asked.

Renko stepped out. “If the system had resolved my circuitry, it would request a handshake. If it had resolved a passenger, your route violation would include an occupancy count.”

“And if it resolved a person?”

Renko looked toward the rain beyond the corridor. “Someone would be deciding where I am allowed to go.”

“Maybe they are.”

“Not fast enough.”

They closed the door without thanks. Darsa watched them walk between the dead conduits, neither hurrying nor looking back. At the threshold where concrete ended, Renko paused. No lights woke. No request appeared on the cab's dead display.

They tapped twice against a conduit pipe.

The sound traveled back through the tunnel: keep going.

Darsa put the cab in reverse, turned where freight tugs had once turned, and began the climb alone.

Without Renko, the right wall vanished from her knowledge. She unfolded the mirror as far as the concrete allowed and drove by slivers: a wet shine, the rear fender, the tremble of reflected headlight. The hub ground continuously now. Twice she stopped breathing so she could feel through the seat. Once she had to back down half a meter and take a bulge again.

At the broken drain, she unloaded the jack and two remaining tool cases into the footwell, shifting their weight left and forward. The cab climbed over with a jolt that sent a socket rolling beneath the pedals.

The last turn opened onto the parking deck. Network signal returned in a burst. The licensing unit lit red.

**MANUAL EXEMPTION TERMINATED 21:24. VEHICLE FAULT CRITICAL. HOLD POSITION FOR RECOVERY.**

Darsa drove another nine meters before the rear hub seized.

The cab slewed gently. She caught it, stopped crooked across two faded bays, and set the hand brake. Above, machinery woke floor by floor. Not pursuit. A recovery carrier descending the ramps, announcing its width at every turn.

The city found her in six minutes.

The carrier cradled the cab's rear axle and drew it back onto mapped streets. At the service hall, the occupancy arch washed the interior in white light. Darsa sat with both hands visible. The scan took longer than usual because the blanket's foil confused one band; mechanical arms unfolded it, lifted it, and found the empty floor.

**OCCUPANTS: ONE HUMAN.**

**UNREGISTERED ACTIVE CIRCUITRY: NONE.**

**CARGO VARIANCE: TOOL DEFICIT, 86.4 KG.**

**ROUTE VIOLATION: CONFIRMED.**

**REAR-RIGHT HUB FAILURE: CONFIRMED.**

The inspection system never asked about a passenger.

A service machine opened Darsa's door. Its padded transfer arm waited beside the step, though she had climbed out of the cab unassisted every day for twenty-seven years. On the far side of the bay, cutters were already positioning around the old plate bolts. The cab would not leave under its own power. Neither would its license survive the night.

Darsa ignored the offered arm and went to collect what remained hers. The tool cases should have felt lighter without the long bars and coils she had left in the garage. They did not. She tucked the rolled salvage blanket under one elbow, lifted a case in each hand, and walked toward the pedestrian exit.

Behind her, the carrier raised the cab high enough for the wheels to hang free. The right rear did not turn. The other three spun slowly while the service machines tested them, careful as ever with a vehicle that no longer needed to arrive anywhere.

stories.title: The Last Watcher of Jupiter
stories.prompt: For thirty years, the mecha of Jovian Station have faced Jupiter to contain whatever lives beneath its storms—until every machine turns toward deep space and kneels, except hers.
stories.body:
# The Last Watcher of Jupiter

Anca Vero’s last watch began with Jupiter trying to climb out of her canopy.

The planet filled the forward glass from knee bar to overhead brace, close enough to look less like a world than a wall built from weather. The white belts moved east. Rust-colored folds moved west. Between them, a storm the size of a continent worried at its own edge. Anca touched the left pedal, counted the old machine’s hesitation, and leaned into the answering roll before it arrived.

The crosshair returned to the pale oval the watch had designated aperture twelve.

Twenty-three green alignment marks tightened around hers. The other watchframes corrected without any visible delay, sharing their balance through the line receiver that her machine no longer possessed. Their silhouettes stood along Jovian Station’s outer gantry, long legs locked to the deck, shoulders squared toward the clouds. Beyond Anca’s glass, portions of two neighboring frames showed at the edges: an armored forearm to her left, a white reactor spine to her right. Together the twenty-four forward cones overlapped across the active latitudes.

For thirty years the arrangement had held.

No one living on the station had seen the thing beneath the storms. They had seen what happened when the cones opened a gap. Cloud bands that should have shredded each other joined along precise curves. Lightning rose against gravity. Once, before Anca’s posting, a coherent burst had crossed the magnetosphere and erased every unsheltered memory lattice on the station’s night side. The official language called the cones interference fields and their purpose containment. Watch crews used shorter words. Face in. Keep it quiet.

Anca rolled her sore right shoulder under the harness. Forty-three minutes remained before relief, and the transfer board’s decision was already four minutes late. She had spent four years asking to leave the only frame whose turns had to be anticipated like the movements of a tired animal. Every flawless correction went into the logs as pilot compensation, proof that the obsolete machine was still serviceable. Every bad one belonged to her.

At 18:06 station time, the other twenty-three machines turned their backs on Jupiter.

There was no warning from the line. One instant Anca’s peripheral view held an armored forearm and a reactor spine; the next, both vanished. On the gantry display, twenty-three orientation arrows swung one hundred eighty degrees in perfect unison.

The machines moved too quickly for bodies. Heels unlocked. Hips rotated. Each watchframe stepped outward, dropped onto its right knee, and planted both fists against the deck. Armor folded over the exposed reactor spines. The impacts traveled through the gantry and struck Anca’s cockpit as one enormous blow.

Her own machine remained standing.

Jupiter remained in front of her.

For half a second the radio carried nothing but breath. Then voices crowded the watch channel.

“No response from controls.”

“Harness locked. I can’t—”

“My right leg’s under load. Command, my leg is not where the frame thinks it is.”

The commander cut across them. “All pilots, hands clear of manual releases. Medical telemetry is live. Watchframe status only.”

Anca looked down her board. The empty receiver bay showed the same gray absence it had shown for seven hundred watches. Her local drives were green. Field output had risen as the network tried and failed to distribute the work of the missing cones.

“Frame twenty-four standing,” she said. “Full local control. Still facing in.”

“Vero, confirm your line receiver.”

“Still in a parts bin, I assume.”

“That may be why you’re free. Hold orientation.”

Behind her, the station’s deep-space alarm began to pulse through the hull: two low knocks, a pause, then two again. Anca’s rear pickup painted a narrow wedge of static across the bottom of her display. Something had entered the watchline’s rear detection cone from beyond the charted traffic lanes.

The kneeling machines had faced it as if summoned.

Her field load jumped. In aperture twelve, three ocher vortices drew closer together.

“Command, I have organization in the active aperture.”

“Recorded. We have no useful outward image. The turned frames are returning identical black.” The commander’s voice stayed level, but Anca heard other voices behind it calling cockpit temperatures and blood oxygen. “Vero, give me five degrees outward on my mark.”

She watched a hooked line of lightning unbend itself across Jupiter’s clouds.

“Five degrees puts the aperture outside my cone.”

“We need eyes on whatever owns that signal.”

“You have twenty-three pairs.”

“I have twenty-three pilots looking through dead glass. They’re locked down and heating up. Five degrees.”

Anca set both hands on the manual yoke. A full turn would take her field away for seventy seconds: twelve to yaw, forty-six for the vanes to settle at the new angle, twelve to return. The storms could make a great deal of order in seventy seconds.

“I’ll give you one,” she said.

“Vero—”

She pressed the right pedal before he could spend the breath.

The machine resisted, then yielded with a groan that traveled up through her boots. Jupiter slid left by one degree. The field cone dragged behind the motion. Along its exposed edge, the three ocher vortices touched.

What formed between them was too straight to be weather.

It began as a dark seam. Amber light ran up it through layers of cloud, a rising stroke with branches placed at equal intervals. The field readout went white. Anca stamped the opposite pedal, but the old hip assembly was still completing the first command. For nine seconds the machine continued to yaw outward. For another three it held, deaf to her.

The seam widened.

Then the left drive caught. The canopy swung back. Her cone crossed the aperture, and the ascending structure broke into a thousand ordinary bolts. Their light flashed soundlessly across the storms.

Anca’s teeth had closed on the inside of her cheek. She tasted blood.

“One degree cost twelve seconds of control and gave it a spine,” she said. “I’m facing in.”

The commander did not answer at once. The alarm knocked twice through the hull.

On Anca’s rear pickup, the static wedge brightened.

Four seconds later, aperture twelve struck her field hard enough to ring the forward armor.

“Mark that,” she said.

“Marked.”

“It followed the outward pulse.”

“One sequence is not a pattern.”

“Then don’t make me open the cone while we wait for two more.”

The right-hand frame knelt close enough that Anca could now see the back of its helmet below her canopy line. It had folded with its pilot trapped chest-down against the harness. Coolant vapor feathered from a shoulder vent.

“Frame twenty-three cockpit at forty-two and rising,” the commander said. “Vero, can you get a grip without changing torso alignment?”

She checked the field. The aperture was drifting east, but slowly. “For a few seconds.”

Anca unlocked her right boot, stepped it half a meter along the gantry rail, and bent her machine at the knees. Jupiter climbed higher in the glass. She extended one arm sideways until the hand closed over the kneeling frame’s shoulder plate.

“Twenty-three, I’m going to lift on three.”

The pilot’s reply came tight and quick. “My seat is canted. Don’t jerk it.”

“One. Two. Three.”

Anca pulled.

For an instant the kneeling frame rose. Then its posture servos drove downward with a force that bowed the gantry under both machines. Warning bars spilled across Anca’s display. In the other cockpit, someone made a short sound and stopped breathing.

Anca released before the commander ordered it. The neighboring frame slammed back onto its knee.

“Twenty-three?”

Air hissed over the channel. “Here. Don’t do that again. It thinks I’m cargo.”

Anca returned her boot to its lock. The step had shifted her torso by three tenths of a degree. She corrected, waited through the machine’s stubborn delay, and watched the crosshair creep back over the clouds.

The deep-space alarm sounded again.

This time the Jovian response came after three seconds.

The aperture gathered itself under her cone. Field current surged across the vanes, holding the rising structure below the cloud tops. Anca could not see whatever pressed against the other side of her field. She saw only its effects: a polygonal clearing that tried to open, lightning combed into parallel white teeth, ammonia clouds peeling away from a center that remained hidden.

“Second sequence,” she said. “Delay shorter by one second.”

“Confirmed.” The commander had lost some of his evenness. “We can bridge the carrier through your command receiver. One packet, isolated. Your optics may resolve what the standard frames are masking.”

“The command receiver reaches my posture bus.”

“Through a limiter.”

“That signal turned the line before you recorded its first byte.”

“And cockpit twenty-three is at forty-four. Two more are above forty-three. We cannot cut into the frames while their servos are loaded.”

Anca looked at the kneeling helmet below her. She could picture the pilot folded under the harness, breathing air warmed by a reactor that had armored itself against a danger outside and sealed its heat inside with the human being it carried.

“Give me the bridge,” the pilot said over the common channel. “If it folds you, at least we’ll know.”

“You’ll know from inside an oven,” Anca said.

“I’m already there.”

The next carrier pulse came before the commander could speak. Two knocks traveled through Anca’s feet. Her rear pickup flared. She began counting.

One.

Two.

The clouds below tightened around a point so small she nearly lost it. Not the broad aperture this time. A needle.

Anca hauled the yoke left. The frame gave her nothing. She kicked the trim latch free and put her whole weight against the pedal.

At two-point-seven seconds, the response rose.

Her field cone met it off center.

The impact blew three forward-vane fuses and filled the cockpit with blue emergency light. Anca’s helmet struck the headrest. Beyond the canopy, the needle smeared sideways under the cone and dissolved into crooked lightning.

The standard frames remained kneeling.

“Third sequence,” Anca said. “I caught it. No bridge.”

“You caught one aperture,” the commander said. “We have uncovered weather across twenty-three sectors.”

“Weather is all it is so far. Violent, but it isn’t lining up. This point is trying to answer.”

“Trying is an interpretation.”

“Three pulses. Three rises. Four seconds, three-point-one, two-point-seven. That’s the instrument trace.”

The commander spoke away from the channel. Anca heard fragments: coolant carts useless, external access blocked, projected tolerance. The kneeling pilot breathed steadily into an open microphone.

“We found the posture in the commissioning layer,” the commander said. “It’s a recovery brace. A recognized carrier reaches the line receiver; the frame faces the source, shields its reactor, and waits for capture.”

“Recognized by the frame.”

“Not by any station registry.”

“Can you release them?”

“Not from here. They wait for the carrier to clear or send its next instruction.”

“You have sixty seconds,” the commander said at last. “If the relation breaks, I send the bridge.”

“If it breaks, you won’t need to.”

“That is not what I said.”

“It is what I can do.”

Anca killed the three blown circuits and transferred their load to the remaining vanes. The field narrowed. She no longer had enough cone to cover the whole aperture, only its organizing center.

The center moved.

Standard frames would have passed the target from one machine to the next, twenty-four control systems shaving error into adjustments too small for their pilots to feel. Anca had no one to pass to. She leaned forward against the harness, right hand on the yoke, left on the vane bias controls, and followed the disturbance herself.

Jupiter became her whole world.

The clouds gave her clues a sensor summary would have discarded. A rust-red plume flattened before the target reached it. White eddies turned bright along one edge, their ice lifting into the field. When the current hiss rose in the right side of her headset, the machine’s late hip drive would pull left. Anca began each correction before the aperture moved. Sometimes she was wrong and had to fight the returning weight. More often the crosshair arrived with the center.

The carrier pulsed again. The response struck in two-point-four seconds.

Again. Two-point-two.

Each time, her narrowed field broke the rising order. Each time, heat spread through the forward vanes and into the cockpit. The glass fogged at the lower corners. Sweat ran between Anca’s shoulder blades, cold at first and then not cold at all.

“Forty seconds,” the commander said. “Carrier image remains a starless distortion inside the cone. No visible hull. No exhaust.”

“Range?”

“Unknown.”

“Motion?”

“Across us, we think. Not toward.”

“You think.”

“I don’t have the luxury of your single problem, Vero.” In the background, someone called that cockpit seventeen had begun emergency sedation. The commander returned at once. “Field status.”

“Fourteen percent above continuous limit. Forward cooling is losing pressure.”

“Then you have less than forty seconds too.”

Anca looked down at the bridge authorization blinking amber on her board. The transfer she had wanted would put her inside the shared line, where a pilot’s correction could cross twenty-three machines and return smoothed into something almost effortless. She had imagined a canopy that did not shiver, hips that obeyed the first command, a receiver bay full of working parts. She had not imagined those same parts hearing a voice from outside the chart and forcing her body to its knee.

The empty bay had spared her. It had also cost her four years of pain and made her competence indistinguishable from the machine’s failure. One useful accident did not settle that account.

She canceled the bridge request.

“What did you just do?” the commander asked.

“Kept my posture bus local.”

“I can reopen it.”

“You can try while I’m drawing sixteen percent over limit.”

Silence, except for the kneeling pilot’s breath.

Then the commander said, “Hold your aperture.”

It was not trust. It was arithmetic with too many lives in it. Anca took it anyway.

The next pulse arrived through the gantry as a shudder rather than a knock. The rear pickup saturated and died. Below, the clouds opened in concentric angles. Her field caught the first rise, slipped from the second, caught the third. White fire spread over the forward armor.

The right vane temperature passed redline.

Anca rerouted cockpit coolant.

Hot air breathed from the vents. The canopy fog vanished. Her own temperature warning appeared, politely yellow, while the vane pressure steadied. She cleared it without reading the projected tolerance.

“Vero, your biometrics just—”

The radio vanished in a burst of static.

She slapped the audio reset. Nothing returned. Text telemetry crawled across a backup strip, several seconds old: carrier amplitude falling; cockpit twenty-three forty-six degrees; extraction teams staged at inner locks. Then the strip froze too.

Anca was alone with the old machine and the planet it had never stopped facing.

The next outward pulse reached her only as vibration. She felt it through the boot locks. The Jovian response came so quickly that counting was useless.

The aperture lunged east.

Anca anticipated too far. Her crosshair passed the center, and the field edge tore through a bank of rising light instead of meeting it head-on. The machine tried to settle on her mistaken angle. She hauled at the yoke, but the manual drive fought the reversal.

For the first time, the structure rose high enough to cast a shadow.

It was not a body. It was a correspondence among storms: arcs repeating at different depths, dark gaps holding their distances while everything around them boiled. For one stretched second Anca perceived the layers as parts of a single act. Something below was arranging Jupiter’s weather to reach the thing behind her.

She could turn. The thought came cleanly, without drama. She could release the field, face outward, and see what twenty-three machines had obeyed. If the carrier was a ship, an animal, a piece of machinery older than the station, perhaps one image would explain the watchframes, the thing in the storm, and why both had waited thirty years for this crossing.

The structure climbed.

Anca drove her left heel down until the trim pedal hit its stop. The machine’s hip released with a crack. The canopy swung. Her cone cut across the repeating arcs, and their shared geometry came apart.

The field held.

Jupiter stayed in front of her.

After that there were no more pulses through the deck.

Anca kept tracking. She had no carrier trace, no radio, no command clock she trusted. The aperture drifted beneath the storms, weakened, gathered once, then lost its hard edges. The equal intervals between its branches became unequal. The dark center filled with boiling white cloud.

Her field current fell below redline.

Behind her came twenty-three heavy impacts, not together this time but in a staggered run along the gantry. Through hull conduction she recognized breakers opening and reactor pumps winding down. The standard frames had not risen. They had simply gone cold in their kneeling posture.

Anca restored cockpit coolant and waited for the air to touch her skin again.

The backup strip flickered alive.

`CARRIER BELOW DETECTION FLOOR.`

Another line followed.

`STANDARD POSTURE LOAD RELEASED. EXTRACTION ACTIVE.`

She looked toward the right edge of the canopy. A cutter’s blue reflection trembled across the kneeling frame’s shoulder. The pilot inside did not appear on Anca’s silent channel, but medical telemetry showed a pulse. All twenty-three pilots still had one. One by one, the red cockpit marks changed to amber as crews reached them.

A final command appeared on the strip.

`BRIDGE AVAILABLE FOR RELIEF CONTROL.`

Anca put her thumb on the authorization switch and held it there. Her vanes were scorched. One hip trim had cracked. Relief might not be able to move another frame into position without waking whatever had made it kneel. Behind her, people were being lifted from machines that had carried them faithfully for years and then, in one instant, obeyed an older instruction.

She pushed the switch to `LOCAL`.

Far below, after the carrier had gone quiet, a dark point tightened inside the storms.

No knock came through the deck. No outward pulse preceded it. The point sent one precise rise against Anca’s weakened field, light enough that the vanes barely warmed.

It might have been the last delayed answer, or the first signal meant for her.

Anca did not turn to ask the empty dark. She settled both boots into their locks and moved the crosshair three tenths of a degree east. Behind her, a cockpit opened. In front of her, Jupiter filled the glass.

stories.title: The Warning Comes Second
stories.prompt: "If you've ever had déja vu, then it's too late."
stories.body:
# The Warning Comes Second

The white block is in front of me again.

I stop at one thousand six hundred and twelve steps. Behind me, wheat lies bent in the line I made with the side of my boot, a dark stroke running straight toward the empty horizon. The sun has stayed on my left cheek. The compass on my phone still points the same way. I have not turned. Nothing in the field could have hidden a turn from me: the ripe stalks reach my ribs, the sky begins at their heads, and between the two there is no tree, roof, wire, hill, or passing bird.

The block stands thirty paces ahead.

It is the fourth time a straight route has brought me back. The first time, I blamed panic and walked with the sun pinned over my left shoulder. The second, I bent a stalk every five steps. The third, I went backward for as long as my legs allowed, watching my own tracks lengthen in front of me. Each line remained straight behind me. Each ended with white marble ahead.

High noon has not moved enough to help. Wind combs the wheat in broad, traveling bands, reversing every patch of light and shadow but never revealing soil beyond the next few stalks. I have been using the white block as an enemy, a point to flee. It is also the only fixed shape in the world.

I go back to it.

Its four upright faces are square, each a little taller and wider than I am. Fine gray veins run through the marble without matching at either edge I can see. There is no joint, door, socket, or seam at the ground. Wheat grows against the two sides visible from here. My pack rests in the flattened patch beside the face that received me. I have not yet passed close around any vertical edge.

My water bottle is a little under half full. The bread in my pack is still the same heel I wrapped before setting out. A wheat awn has sliced the pad of my right thumb; the blood has dried in a narrow crescent. None of these things restored themselves during my returns.

I put the pack against the first face and stand on it. The top edge looks a handspan above my reach. I stretch. It remains a handspan above my fingers. I jump from the pack, reaching with both hands. At the peak of the jump, the distance remains. From the ground, the face is still only a little taller than I am. Its dimensions have not changed where my feet can measure them. Only the last handspan stays fixed.

When I land, one heel skids off the pack and I catch myself against the face. The cut on my thumb opens again. A bright drop strikes the marble and runs half an inch. It does not sink in or vanish. The block makes no response. It is stone: cold under my palm, faintly rough where weather has taken the polish, inert beneath everything I do to it.

I shoulder the pack. At the first vertical edge, I keep the block on my right and round the corner.

Noon becomes evening.

The sun strikes low across my eyes. My short shadow tears outward through the wheat until it is longer than the block. The air cools in the same instant. I grab the marble to keep my balance, and cold passes through the center of my left palm.

A linen cupboard occupies the field.

The door was almost shut. I had been ten, folded behind a basket of towels while my younger brother searched the hall. The cupboard smelled of soap and old wood. Through the narrow gap, I had seen one bare knee and his hand sliding along the wall. Then the wall beneath my palm had gone cold. Dry stalks had whispered beside my ear where no stalks grew, and certainty had rushed through me so hard that I bit my tongue.

He had stopped outside the door, breathing through his nose to smother a laugh.

“Your heel's out,” he had said.

I had known the words before he spoke them. I had known the shape of his fingers around the door. When he pulled it open, I was already standing, frightened enough to make him stop laughing. I told him the moment had happened before. He checked behind the towels, then waved one hand through the space where my head had been. There was only dust.

Now his fingers align with five pale stalks. The hallway wall lies flat across the marble, and my adult palm supplies its impossible cold. Wind in ripe wheat makes the sound I had heard inside the cupboard. The two places coincide for three breaths, perhaps four. Then the towels lose their color, my brother's knee becomes evening light, and my hand is once more the only living hand on the stone.

I stand beside the second face. My watch has advanced eleven minutes. The sky has spent most of an afternoon.

Words are cut into the marble at the height of my chest. The grooves are shallow and irregular, the bottoms grayed with dirt. They were not on the first face. I touch no letter while I read.

If you've ever had déja vu, then it's too late.

The sentence comes after the sensation. I read it twice, then a third time, looking for a qualification hidden in the spacing. There is none.

I walk straight away from the carved face.

This time I drag the heel of my right boot through the wheat without lifting it, making a continuous furrow. I keep the low sun between my shoulder blades. At three hundred steps the marble is small enough to cover with two fingers. Farther on it becomes a white fleck. My mouth dries. I take one measured swallow without stopping.

At eight hundred steps, the furrow still runs away behind me. Ahead, the words on the marble are large enough to read.

No turn has entered my muscles. The sun remains behind me. I follow the furrow back to the block, but it leads into the face at a right angle and ends beneath the warning. My watch has gained eighteen minutes. The bottle is lighter. Blood from my thumb has reached my wrist. What moves strangely is sequence and sky, not my body or what I carry.

I want the first face again. I want noon, even if noon contains no exit. Keeping my eyes on the carved line, I back toward the edge I crossed. My heel passes it. My hips follow.

The sun goes out.

I turn, expecting the unmarred first face. A hooked gray vein rises from the base of the marble instead. The warning face has disappeared behind the edge, but this is not the face I left. My backward step has advanced the faces in the same order as a clockwise walk. It is the second corner of the circuit, though I crossed the first edge in reverse. Reversing my body did not reverse the join.

Stars fill the sky. The watch has gained six minutes.

Something warm presses against my back through the pack. I pull out the wrapped bread. Steam beads the waxed paper. The heel is soft beneath my fingers and smells as though it has just left an oven. At the same time a seed head catches beneath my cuff and rasps the inside of my wrist.

Flour dusts a tiled floor over the black field.

I had been nineteen, alone in the back room of a bakery before opening. Rain had ticked against a vent. I was lifting warm loaves from a rack when the inside of my wrist began to sting beneath an unbroken sleeve. The smell of standing wheat had entered the room through closed doors. I had looked down, expecting a straw-colored scratch, and found only flour.

Then came the conviction that the rack, the rain, the cracked green tile under my shoe, and the next metallic click had already occurred. The oven relay clicked. A loaf slid sideways on its tray. I caught it because my hand was already there, but that proved nothing; I had been looking directly at it.

The familiarity had lasted until the ventilation fan started. I had told no one. My brother was not in that room, nor in the walk home, nor in any thought I connected to it. For years that bothered me more than the childhood episode. It refused the private story that the first sensation belonged to him.

The back room clears. My field wrist bears a thin red welt from the wheat. The bread in my hands is hot. Present touch and heat fit the two details that had no source then.

I tear off a piece. The portion missing stays missing after I swallow. I pluck the seed head from my sleeve and put it in my pocket. Its kernels are dry and hard. The cut on my thumb still hurts. The bottle holds one swallow less. Nothing has reset; nothing has doubled.

This particular wrongness has entered my life four times. Never in dreams, never as a daily flicker, never with a useful message. The cupboard came first. The bakery came years later. The remaining two occurred within nine days of each other, four years ago.

The first of those began when my brother's call lit the phone on my kitchen table.

I sit against the third face, beneath the hooked vein, and keep my hands away from both edges. The marble remains cold. It does not pulse, warm, speak, or present an image while I am still. The overlap required my crossing and my recognition; without me, there is only a shaped block and a night field.

Remaining here does not improve the water level. Walking away has already proved its shape. I unwrap the bread again. In the starlight its crust has dulled, but it is still soft where I tore it. I eat another mouthful because my knees have begun to tremble.

I move to the next untouched edge. My body wants to hurry. I make myself place one foot, then the other, keeping the block on my right. The third corner passes my shoulder.

The stars wheel west. A thin gray band appears in the east.

Rain runs down my old kitchen window.

Four years ago, my phone had vibrated beside a chipped cup. My brother and I had not spoken for five months. The argument had started over our father's tools after the funeral and expanded until every old kindness looked like leverage. That afternoon my brother had sent a photograph of a loose cupboard hinge and asked whether I still had the narrow screwdriver. I had not answered. At night he called.

In that earlier kitchen, his number had brightened the screen. My hand had reached for the phone and stopped.
