Julian paused with the broom. “For what it’s worth, I didn’t ask either. I heard angel and started pointing at things.”

“You did,” Coralie said.

He nodded, took the dustpan from its hook, and went back to work.

Tomas pulled out a chair but did not sit. “What do you need me to understand tonight?”

The narrowness of it helped. Not everything. Not forever. Tonight.

“That not making me explain myself isn’t the same as leaving room for me to tell you.”

His fingers tightened around the chair back. “All right.”

“And don’t say it doesn’t matter.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were.”

“I was going to say it doesn’t change why we’re married.”

Julian made a small sound and became extremely interested in crumbs beneath the table.

Coralie looked at Tomas. “Why are we married?”

He answered too quickly. “Because I love you.”

She waited.

Tomas exhaled. “Because you came back after our first dinner, even though I burned the rice and blamed the pot. Because you ask for what you want until I stop pretending I can’t hear it.” His gaze dropped to the badly folded foil at the counter. “You remember the lemon and the pepper, and you still lose your keys twice a week. I wanted all of it. I still do.”

Coralie’s throat tightened, which was inconvenient but not persuasive by itself.

“Those are reasons,” she said. “They don’t answer what you thought I was.”

“No.” Tomas sat at last. “They don’t.”

He did not reach for another defense. That mattered.

Julian finished sweeping and carried the dustpan to the bin. On his return, he lifted the last two chairs onto the bread table. He kept his eyes on the chair legs.

“I can lock the rear door,” he said.

“Please,” Coralie said.

He checked the door, turned off the kitchen light, and collected his coat. At the front entrance he hesitated, visibly searching for something that might release them all from the evening.

Nothing arrived.

“I’ll bring the good coffee next week,” he said.

“Not the dark roast,” Tomas said.

Julian looked at Coralie.

“Not the dark roast,” she agreed.

He left.

The hall felt larger without him, though he had never occupied much space. Tomas checked the stove. Coralie counted the leftover cartons. They worked separately, not performing anger and not pretending it had passed. When Tomas reached for her coat, he held it open low enough that she could guide her wings through the split back herself.

Outside, rain had thinned to a cold mist. Their building stood one block away. On clear nights Coralie sometimes flew that block for the pleasure of landing on their roof, but wet feathers doubled the work, and her left wing had been trembling since the man came back for his cap.

Tomas walked on her right, the side where the pavement narrowed around three overfilled bins. He did not take her elbow. He only moved outward so she had room.

At the corner he said, “Was any of my guess close?”

Coralie watched rain bead on the barbs of her outer feathers. “Close in appearance.”

He waited.

“Not in flight.” She tucked the wing in before it struck a signpost. “The wings do the work, but they aren’t all of it. If I’m emptied out, muscle won’t get me off the ground.”

“Emptied out how?”

“I can’t give you a useful answer yet.”

“All right.” After half a block he asked, “Does anything help?”

“Quiet first. Then hot tea.”

He nodded.

In their entryway, Tomas turned on the lamp and went past the kettle without touching it. Coralie hung her coat, took the wooden comb from the shelf, and held it out to him.

He accepted it by the handle. “Long feathers?”

She opened her left wing across the room, leaving him just enough space to kneel beside it.

“Start at the outside,” she said.

stories.title: The Anatomy of a God
stories.prompt: "You actually managed to counteract my regeneration?" "I don't know what your deal is, but where I am from guys like you aren't rare, hell, my stepsister is one of you. We know how to deal with your anathomy." "What are you talking about!? I am a GOD!" "You have the ego of one, that's for sure"
stories.body:
# The Anatomy of a God

The man I had stabbed stopped being dead before I reached my satchel.

I do not use *dead* loosely. I had spent twelve years with my hands on people at their worst—under fallen masonry, in fever cots, on kitchen floors after a regeneration went wrong. I knew the little concessions a body made before it quit. His had made all of them. No breath. No pulse against my knuckles. Eyes fixed on the painted beams of the sanctuary while rain worried at the roof.

Then the wound under his torn coat drew itself shut. It did not glow. There was no choir, no clean flash of divine correction. The flesh tightened in small, ugly increments, as if invisible fingers were pulling a purse string. His ribs lifted. One heel scraped the audience floor. Heat rolled off him strongly enough to stir the dust between us.

My satchel lay where he had thrown it, six paces away beside the outward doors. The doors were still barred. The broken ceremonial knife was in my hand, its edge dark to the hilt. I backed toward the satchel.

The man sat up.

Rainwater tapped through the high windows and collected in copper bowls along the walls. He looked first at the knife, then at me. His face had returned to its grave, handsome arrangement, but the eyes did not track together at once. The left caught me. The right wandered to the empty dais and came back.

“You were told to kneel,” he said.

“You put your hand on my neck.”

“I showed you the posture.”

He rose before his balance had returned. His right knee locked. His weight went too far toward that side, and one bare foot slapped down to save him. He disguised the correction by spreading his arms, turning a stumble into benediction.

I had seen my stepsister do the same thing with a tray of soup. She had come home from a roof collapse with every bone apparently mended and no idea where the floor intended to be. She took three majestic steps into the kitchen, raised the tray as though presenting it to a court, and fell shoulder-first into the flour bin.

*Don’t laugh,* she had said from inside the white cloud.

*I’m getting a cloth.*

*You’re laughing while you get it.*

The man before me had no flour on his face and would not have improved with it. Still, the resemblance gave me a place to start. Not certainty. I had made that mistake before.

I nudged one of the copper bowls with my heel. It skated over the tiles, ringing, and spilled rainwater across his path.

His gaze followed it a fraction late. I ran for the satchel.

He moved fast once he chose a direction. His hand closed on the shoulder of my coat just as I caught the satchel strap. I dropped my weight, turned beneath his arm, and dragged the broken knife across the back of his forearm. His grip opened. The cut began closing even as his blood struck the floor.

“Again?” he asked, his eyebrows lifting.

“I only need the door.”

“There is no door for you until you acknowledge whose house received you.”

“This house tried to drown me through the ceiling.”

I pulled the satchel toward me. He stamped on the trailing strap.

The sanctuary had been empty when I climbed to it from the ravine road: no attendants, no pilgrims, no smoke from the kitchens. Only this man seated above a hall of mildewed cushions, waiting in a dry circle while the storm came over the mountain. I had asked for shelter. He had asked for my knees. We had both repeated ourselves until he decided to demonstrate.

Now a tendon stood out in his neck. His renewed skin shone with sweat. He noticed me looking and lifted his chin.

“You witnessed death obey me.”

“I witnessed you get very hot.”

I jerked the strap sideways. His foot shifted, and the satchel came free. Two buckles burst. Rolls of bandage, three stoppered vials, my shears, and a coil of recovery web scattered over the floor.

He looked down. I looked at the doors behind him.

“No,” he said.

That was his first useful answer. I snatched up the coil and ran the other way, toward the faded curtain beside the dais. Behind it, a narrow service stair dropped into the mountain. The smell rising from below was wet stone, old leather, and minerals sharp enough to taste.

The road would be under water soon. My satchel was open on the audience floor. The sensible path was behind a man who had already survived being killed once.

I took the stairs.

He followed without hurry at first. His bare feet made soft, deliberate sounds above me.

“You came into my refuge,” he called. “You drew blood beneath my image.”

There had been paintings on the hall walls. Damp had peeled most faces away, leaving crowns afloat over pale smears.

“Is that who they were meant to be?” I asked.

The steps turned sharply. I slipped around the central support and waited. When his shoulder appeared, I cast the recovery web over his arm, braced one heel against the stair, and pulled his wrist toward the opposite hip.

It was the first hold we used when my stepsister’s repairs ran too fast. Her body mended along two broad chains that crossed through her trunk. When both tried to bear weight at once, they dragged her into a spasm strong enough to break whatever she was lying on. We never stopped the repair. We gave one chain work and asked the other to rest.

The web drew taut. The man’s shoulder turned; his left leg faltered.

For half a breath, I thought I had him. Then his hip moved the wrong way.

Not wrong for him. Wrong for my hands. Instead of unwinding across the body, the tension climbed his right side and vanished beneath his ribs. He seized the web and hauled. I hit the underside of the stair hard enough to burst sparks across my sight.

He twisted his captured arm. The wrist folded where the web held it. I released by instinct, but he had already used the injury to slip the loop. By the time his hand closed around the central support, the joint had rebuilt.

He pulled the web from me and snapped its wooden tension bar against the wall.

“A net,” he said. His breath was quicker now. “Was that the breadth of your revelation?”

I pushed myself upright. “No.”

“What, then?”

I said nothing. He wanted an answer more than he wanted me caught. That bought me two steps.

The stair ended at a landing lined with body braces.

They stood in pairs, tall frames of blackened wood with padded slings for shoulders and hips. Some were child-sized. Others could have held the man above me with room to spare. Their leather was cracked, their buckles green, but grooves had been worn into the handrails by years of use. A shelf held empty salt jars and cups with mineral crust around their rims.

So the great audience hall had a hidden underside, and somebody had once spent a great deal of time helping bodies through difficult hours.

The man stopped on the last stair. He saw where I was looking.

“Those are refuse.”

“Good. I need parts.”

I tore a sound length of strap from the nearest frame. He came down fast.

I ducked behind the brace. His fist split the upper rail where my head had been. The old wood gave way with a dry report. I caught the lower rail and drove the broken frame across his shins. He kicked through it; one upright glanced off his left hip. His right shoulder tightened after the hip had already taken the force, while his right knee corrected into the pull beneath his ribs. The delayed eye, the locked knee, the staggered response—none of it made my stepsister’s clean crossing. His repair carried load in offset pairs, overlapping instead of mirroring.

Or I was frightened and inventing patterns because patterns were easier than death.

He caught my coat again and lifted me against the wall.

“Look at me,” he said.

Up close, his skin smelled of hot metal and rain. The corner of his mouth ticked. He had spent water sealing what I had opened, then spent more escaping the web.

“I am looking.”

“What do you see?”

His grip tightened. He expected an office, a domain, a glorious name. I saw one pupil wider than the other and salt dried white below his ear.

I drove my thumb into the knot already trembling under his renewed arm. The arm folded before the rest of him caught up. I dropped, left my coat in his hand, and ran through the low doorway at the end of the landing.

The chamber beyond was round and warm. A mineral basin occupied its center, fed by a pipe that dripped cloudy water from the rock. Four iron supports leaned over it. Straps hung from them, better preserved by the damp than the frames outside. Against the far wall, a maintenance gate stood above a drainage channel. Rain showed silver through its slats—an exit, if the wheel would turn.

I reached it and put both hands on the wheel. Rust flaked beneath my palms. It shifted one finger’s width, then stopped.

Behind me, water splashed.

The man had stepped into the basin. He crouched and drank from his hands, without ceremony now. The tremor in his face eased. His shoulders settled at different times, right before left. The bruise at his left hip faded upward toward his right shoulder while the scrape at his right knee contracted toward his ribs. Not a crossing. Two crooked lines sharing the middle.

My stepsister had once woken me after midnight by tapping a spoon against my doorframe.

*Cup’s too heavy,* she said.

It was not. The cup was tin. But her repairs had spent everything after a fever, and both hands shook when she tried to lift it.

*Water or broth?*

*Water. No, broth. Is there any salt left?*

I had held the cup while she drank. In the morning, when she could close her fingers again, she made me practice the release buckle on the recovery web until I could open it with either hand. The first time I fumbled, she took the web away. If I could not open it frightened and half-awake, she said, I had no business closing it around her.

The man rose from the basin.

“Last opportunity,” he said.

His words came more slowly, perhaps because he had decided slow speech sounded merciful. His attention had sharpened. He was done displaying himself.

I let go of the gate wheel. “All right.”

He waited.

I lowered myself to one knee.

Satisfaction altered his face before he could prevent it. He stepped out of the basin and came to stand over me. Water streamed from his clothes. His right foot landed close to my hand, his weight already committed forward.

I pulled the release pin from the nearest support.

The iron arm dropped across his right shoulder. I rose under it, using my legs and his forward motion to drive him past me. He struck the basin rail. Before he could turn, I looped a broad strap behind that shoulder and clipped it to the rear support.

He tore the clip free.

I had expected him to. The break dragged his shoulder backward while his left hip drove forward to recover his balance. I kicked the second support loose. Its padded sling caught the hip and held that rotation for one crucial moment.

His renewal answered the strain. Heat struck my face.

The line from his left hip to his right shoulder tightened first, trying to set both into one bearing posture. The fading injury at his right knee called the line beneath his ribs a beat later and turned his trunk against it. I pulled the remaining strap low across the basin, not around a joint but across the two slings, and fed it through the old floor ring.

He reached for me. His fingers brushed my hair.

I threw my whole weight backward.

The slings turned in opposite directions.

He could have broken either one with ordinary strength. He tried. The right shoulder surged forward; the left hip followed; the half-mended knee asked him to shift back. His body corrected the correction. One foot stamped down and did not rise. His reaching hand stopped short of my throat.

The chamber filled with the smell of hot stone.

“What did you do?” The ceremonial fullness had gone out of his voice.

I kept both hands on the strap. It thrummed hard enough to numb my fingers. “Held the repairs apart.”

He heaved again. The iron supports groaned. A buckle tore halfway through its leather tab, then stopped when his strength vanished into another shudder.

“My renewal.” He pulled once, weaker. “You stopped it.”

“Not for long.”

He stared at the motionless hand in front of him. His mouth opened, but no sound came until he tried the hand again. “How?”

I watched his breathing. Fast, but open. The strap had not crossed his throat or chest. Good.

“Where I come from, regenerators aren’t rare.”

His mouth tightened around the word as though I had called him livestock.

“My stepsister is one,” I added. “I guessed you’d be similar. You weren’t. Not quite.”

He tested the bind with a small turn of the shoulder. The strap hummed.

“I am a god.”

“You keep saying that.” My grip slipped. I wrapped the loose end once around my forearm and leaned back. “Stop pulling.”

“Release me.”

“When I’m outside.”

He fought the bind again. The right support lifted from the floor and slammed down. Heat poured from him, but there was nowhere for the effort to go except through the mismatched renewal. His legs buckled without letting him fall. The slings held him in a strained half-kneel at the basin’s edge.

“You mistake the body for the being,” he said through his teeth.

“I’m working on the part that grabbed me.”

His eyes found mine. For the first time since he rose upstairs, he was not performing for an invisible hall. He was measuring distance, buckles, my tired hands. Thinking. The change made him more dangerous and easier to predict.

“How long?” he asked.

“If you keep doing that? I don’t know.”

“And if I stop?”

“Lie still. Let the heat come down. The straps loosen when your body quits choosing between the two positions.”

“You expect obedience.”

“No. I’m telling you what happens next.”

The damaged buckle gave a small, fibrous creak.

He could keep fighting until the old leather failed. He might catch me before his next collapse. Or he could preserve his body by accepting stillness from a stranger who had already proved willing to stab him. Neither choice resembled worship.

His hand closed by a fraction. Opened. At last he let his shoulder sink into the sling.

The strap went on vibrating for several breaths, then softened.

I waited until his weight settled without another surge. Releasing my end too quickly could tighten the hip sling; leaving it wound around my arm meant he could drag me close if he changed his mind. I unwound one turn at a time.

“Your people built this room for the aftereffects,” I said. It was not a question.

He looked toward the salt jars on the landing. “They feared imperfection.”

Maybe they had. Maybe they had simply grown tired of catching him when the floor moved. I did not need his version before the road vanished.

I secured the strap with the release buckle facing his free hand. He could reach it once the tremor passed. Then I took a cup from the shelf, filled it at the basin pipe, and set it on the rim near him.

He watched the cup instead of me.

“That is not reverence,” he said.

“It’s water.”

I went upstairs for my things.

He did not call after me. In the audience hall, the rain had found new holes. It drummed on the scattered contents of my satchel, soaked the bandages, and washed his blood into the cracks between the tiles. I recovered the vials, the shears, and what dry wrapping remained. The broken knife I left beneath his painted faces.

The outward doors still would not open. I returned to the recovery chamber and forced the maintenance wheel with the shears wedged through its spokes. Rust cracked. The gate lifted six inches, then nine, spilling cold rain over my boots.

Behind me, the man remained still. Steam had stopped rising from his coat.

“There are many of me?” he asked.

The question was quieter than his other questions and less complete.

I crouched by the opening and pushed my satchel through. “Many who mend. I don’t know if any of them are you.”

His lips parted, then closed.

I slid under the gate and dropped onto the lower slope.

The ravine road had already flooded. Brown water covered the marker stones and shouldered branches against the bend. Going down would put me in the river before dark; going back through the sanctuary would put me in front of its owner before his hands steadied.

Above the road, a goat track cut across the shale toward the ridge, narrow, exposed, and still passable. I shortened the satchel strap. Before the rain loosened it, I put my full weight onto the first slab and started up.

stories.title: Friends of the Night
stories.prompt: While your predecessors were busy hunting the beasts that hid in the shadows, you decided to befriend them. And when war came to your lands, your enemies found their armies shrinking in the night.
stories.body:
# Friends of the Night

At sunset I set two river eels on the flat stone and backed away twelve paces.

Crooktail watched from under the hazels. I knew it by the right angle in its tail and the pale seam along one forepaw, though neither mark showed until it chose to move. Shadow beasts were not made of darkness. They had ribs, burrs in their fur, mud between their broad toes. Crooktail even sneezed when the hazels flowered. But its coat held so little light that my eye kept losing the edges of it, and when it lowered its head the ground seemed to open a mouth.

For six years, this had been our measure. I brought eels or a hare's liver. I struck the stone once with a hazel switch. Sometimes Crooktail ate while I sat nearby. Sometimes it left me to the flies. Once it had followed me almost to the lower gate, pausing whenever I turned, and for a month afterward I had called that proof of friendship. Then I learned that a slaughterhouse cart had dripped blood along the same road.

That evening it did not look at the eels. Its ears had turned toward the western rim.

Drums came over the ridge, softened by distance but too regular for thunder. One by one, points of fire appeared above the barley fields. They multiplied down the road until the rim of Shalegate looked stitched with red thread.

Crooktail withdrew under the hazels. The brush gave one dry shiver, then nothing.

“Tavik!” Torma called from the fort wall. “Inside. Now.”

By the time I reached the gate, the western host had begun pouring into the valley: pikes first, then wagons and horse, all taking their places with the dull competence of people who expected to sleep on conquered ground. Torma stood above the arch in a boiled-leather coat, counting standards. Beside her, Denek was unhooding the east beacon.

“Leave that covered,” I said.

Denek did not turn. “A dark wall is an invitation.”

“A high flame will throw every sentry's shadow across the beast runs.”

Torma leaned over the parapet. “How far?”

“On level ground? Thirty paces, perhaps more. It depends on the flame and where they're moving.”

“Can you keep them off the wall?”

“No.”

She waited. Torma had a way of leaving silence open until a weak answer walked into it and died. I gave her no second answer.

“Light the beacons,” she said. “Double water beside each. Tavik, mark every run you know. Denek, keep the lower ward off them.”

The old keeper struck flint. “That was always the rule.”

Pitch caught with a greasy cough. Light vaulted over the inner roofs, and our shadows sprang westward along the wall.

The first man shrank before the enemy finished pitching its command tent.

He was an east-wall sentry carrying a bundle of quarrels. One moment his boots thudded above me; the next came a small metal clatter, no louder than a dropped cup. I found him hanging from the drain groove in the wall walk, his fingers hooked over its edge. He, his coat, his sword and the bundle on his back had all dwindled together. I could have covered his body with both hands.

“Don't pull,” he gasped as I reached for him. “The buckle's caught.”

That was our first good fact: the change had not hurt him, and fear had not taken his sense. I freed the buckle with my knife and lowered him into my cap.

Below the wall, Crooktail stood on the bare run with its jaw closed around the sentry's long black shadow. There was no tearing, no blood. The shadow narrowed between its teeth like cloth drawn through a ring. Then Crooktail released it and vanished under the thorn fence.

A shout rose from the enemy's near pickets. Another followed, farther south. Torches moved, stooped, scattered. By midnight our scouts had brought in five diminished soldiers they had found struggling through grass that reached their shoulders.

One of Torma's spearmen looked down at the captives. “What do we do with these?”

“Get a bread tray,” I said.

“I meant after.” His boot shifted closer.

Torma caught the back of his belt and hauled him one step away. “After, you obey the law. Bread tray.”

The captives were cold, furious, and too frightened to sit still. We put the east-wall sentry with them because he refused to be carried alone. Under shielded lamps, which cast no useful reach for a beast's jaws, I checked each of them. Armor rivets, scabbards, bootlaces: all reduced in proportion. A picket's dropped torch had remained full-sized where it fell.

“How do you undo it?” Torma asked.

“The shepherd boy who shrank three winters ago recovered beyond the north ledge.”

“That boy was delirious.” Denek folded his arms. “He told us a moon spoke to him.”

“The moon did not return his height. Distance did.”

“You hope.”

“I observed.”

Torma pointed to the friendly sentry in my cap. “Take him to the ledge. If he grows, come back before dawn. If he doesn't, keep going.”

The north path stayed behind the fort and climbed out of the beasts' feeding range. Denek came with me, a spear in one hand and the tiny sentry's bundle in the other. He repeated the old rules as we walked: flame high and close, stone underfoot, no reaching into brush. I knew them. I had learned them from him before I learned how many beasts his drives had killed.

At the third boundary cairn, the cap jerked in my hands. I set it down just in time. The sentry unfolded out of it, first the size of a child, then of a man crouching naked in the cold, except that his clothes and gear were growing with him. His sword knocked over two stones. Denek jumped back and leveled the spear.

The sentry lay panting on the path. “Can I stand now?”

“Try your left foot first,” Denek said.

He could stand. He was hungry and shaking, but whole.

On the way down, Denek carried the cap.

At noon, Torma met the invaders under a white shield hung from a pike. She took me because I knew the beasts, and Denek because he knew when I mistook a wish for a fact.

Marshal Drost arrived with six guards and a clerk. He wore bronze scales over blue wool. The guards wore no open flame, and all of them watched the grass. Behind them, soldiers were raising siege frames while carpenters measured our gate.

“Six pickets are missing,” Drost said. His voice still had ceremony in it. “You will return them and remove the affliction.”

“Five are inside,” Torma said. “The sixth ran west after he changed. We did not catch him.”

Drost looked at me. “You are the keeper.”

“I keep people from crossing the runs. I don't keep the beasts.”

“Then you have failed at the smaller task.”

“You brought twelve hundred open flames into their range.”

His clerk glanced down at the tablet before him. Drost did not. “One thousand eight hundred and forty-two. Your wall has perhaps four hundred fit defenders.”

“Four hundred and six,” Torma said. “All behind stone.”

I crouched and drew the valley in the dust: fort, barley fields, western road, outer ridge. “Put out the fires. Withdraw on this road. Beyond the ridge, your people recover.”

“You have tested that?”

“One man, northward.”

“Your man.”

“The beasts caught him under our beacon. They don't know your colors.”

For the first time, Drost looked toward the wall instead of through us. Then he wiped out my road with the toe of his boot.

“Nets at every fire,” he told the clerk. “Two handlers to each. Widen the fire lines by dusk.”

“Longer shadows give them more to reach,” I said.

“And more light gives my handlers something to see.”

Torma lifted the white shield from the pike. “Your five soldiers will be set outside the south gate at sundown. That is the last courtesy you get in my fields.”

We walked back without speaking until the gate shut behind us.

Denek stopped under the arch. “He is doing what we did.”

“You used hounds and hooked poles.”

“We used beacons first.” He rubbed his thumb along the old spear shaft. “Beacon nights pulled the beasts toward the outer houses. Shadows crossed beds, cradles, doorways. People ran small into winter rain. We killed the beasts because we could not move the wall.”

I had heard the death counts. I had dressed them in my own explanation: frightened keepers, ignorant hunters, an easy cruelty inherited as custom. “You told me they came into the houses.”

“They did. After our light laid a road to them.”

“And you kept lighting it.”

“There were raiders then too.” Denek looked up at the blazing east beacon. “Darkness never promised to spare us, Tavik.”

Neither had Crooktail. That was the part I had made soft in my mind.

When I took Denek's post, I shuttered the house lamps, moved slaughter scraps away from the lanes, and cut new runs toward the stream. The drives ended. No resident had shrunk in six years. I had called that friendship because I needed a word better than truce and warmer than successful drainage.

The second night showed me the limit of all three words.

Drost's bonfires made noon-colored islands across the valley. Each soldier standing near them cast a black road forty or fifty paces long. Nets lay open beside the flames. At first the handlers laughed when small shapes flickered at the edges. Then the shapes crossed between fires, and men began dropping below the line of shields.

A pike company collapsed unevenly as shadows passed over the south run. One soldier dropped to knee height; another dwindled until the grass hid him. Their clothes and weapons changed with them, but the ladders they held did not. Timber crashed. Horses reared above riders suddenly too small to manage reins. Orders broke apart into names and warnings.

From the wall I counted seven beasts. Then ten. Then I found the crook in one tail.

Crooktail had entered a net beside the largest fire. The handlers dragged the corners tight and pinned them with hooked stakes. Crooktail rolled, silent, while flame lit the pale seam of its paw. Every struggle wound the mesh closer around its throat.

“Open the lower gate,” I told Torma.

“No.” She was moving archers away from the long beacon shadows as she answered. “That camp is folding without us.”

“The beasts are trapped between their fires and ours. Douse the wall. Give them dark to leave through.”

“If I douse it, I lose the barley approach.”

Another ladder fell in the camp. Someone screamed for water; someone else screamed not to bring a torch.

Denek joined us at the parapet. “No dark gate during siege,” he said. “Keep the flame high. Keep stone under your feet.”

“Can you reach that net?” Torma asked him.

He watched the fire, the ditch and the folds of ground between. His lips moved once, repeating distances. “By the old drive path. Two men, no lamp.”

“Take Tavik.” She turned to the beacon crews. “Hood the east. Then the south. Lower gate opens one body wide, and it shuts behind them.”

The wall went dark in sections. Each vanished beacon erased a row of roofs, then joined the space between fort and field into one deep black. Wind carried sparks from Drost's camp, but the beasts now had somewhere the long fire-shadows did not reach.

Denek and I slipped out.

He led without hesitation. “My shoulder,” he whispered. “Stay level with it.”

“I can see the ditch.”

“Good. Don't step in it.”

The old drive path bent through thorn gaps I had never noticed because Denek's hunters had cut them to funnel fleeing beasts. Twice he put a hand against my chest and stopped me before a shadow swept across us. Once a diminished soldier blundered into my shin and clung there.

“Road west,” I whispered, turning him by the shoulders. “No fire.”

He stumbled away without answering.

At the largest bonfire, the world became glare and hard edges. Crooktail's net was fixed to four stakes. One handler had shrunk inside his own loop of rope; the other had fled. Denek crawled behind a supply chest, reached the first anchor and sawed through it with his belt knife.

I smothered a fallen torch under my coat. The shadow attached to Denek's hand vanished an instant before a beast snapped at it.

“That's one,” he said. His voice was steady, but he cut the next rope too fast and nicked his thumb.

The net loosened. Crooktail twisted, baring teeth no darker than ordinary teeth. Mesh still cinched its hindquarters to the last two anchors.

Boots approached from the fire side. At first I expected a child. Then I saw the bronze scales, each one reduced to the size of my thumbnail.

Drost stood no higher than my shoulder. Two guards flanked him, one scarcely reaching his waist. Rank had not left his face, but ceremony had.

“Three hundred eleven changed,” he said. “Forty-eight cannot clear the wagon ruts. Seventeen are missing. How long?”

“Until they cross the western ridge.”

“How long until more change?”

A shadow beast worried at a darkness stretched from the far fire. A soldier beside it dropped below the height of the supply chest.

“As long as you make those shadows,” I said.

Drost looked at the net. “This one leads them?”

“No.”

“You feed it.”

“It comes when it chooses.”

“Then why are you here?”

The final rope creaked as Crooktail strained. Denek shifted his knife into a stabbing grip, not toward the beast. Drost noticed.

“Because I know this one,” I said. “Cut that anchor, put out every fire, and I can mark your road. Torma can keep our bows on the wall. Those are the pieces I have.”

“No guarantee?”

“The boundary restored our sentry. I won't promise what the beasts do between here and it.”

Drost's smaller guard raised his spear. “Marshal, we can take them.”

“You can reach his knee,” Drost said. “Lower it.”

He drew a short bronze knife, stepped onto the loose edge of the net and cut the last anchor himself. Denek severed the remaining cord. Crooktail came free in a rush. It struck my shoulder, knocked me into the ash and crossed the firelight without looking back. The other beasts followed its movement only because open ground had appeared ahead of it, a scattering of black bodies choosing the same dark.

Drost watched them go. “Take me to your captain.”

Torma would not open the gate for him. She spoke through the waist-high wicket while Drost stood outside with Denek and me. A shielded lamp inside gave her enough light to see our faces and threw no shadow past the threshold.

“Engines stay,” she said. “Pikes stacked in the west field. Every open flame out. Your first file moves before the next dusk is gone.”

“I have three hundred eleven diminished and seventeen uncounted.”

“Find them by daylight.”

“I need two wagons for those who cannot keep pace.”

“Take wagons. Not towers, rams or throwers.”

“My host does not leave its sidearms.”

Torma considered that. “Sidearms stay sheathed until you're past the ridge. One drawn blade, we close the road.”

Drost's jaw tightened. “Your archers could cut us apart at the boundary.”

“They could cut you apart now.”

“Not before my full-sized ranks reach your gate.”

“Then we're both still counting.” Torma bent to hear a report from someone behind her, answered it, then returned. “You get one daylight. No fire tonight, no fire tomorrow. Departure at dusk.”

Drost did his own counting in silence. Supply intervals, walking speed, the time needed to lower the siege lines without flame: I could see the numbers replacing anger because numbers were ground he trusted.

“At dusk,” he said.

The third day passed under a pale sky. Drost's soldiers dismantled nothing they could not carry. They left the siege engines standing like stripped trees and stacked pikes in the barley. Torma's archers watched from the dark wall. Some asked why we did not fire while the enemy was broken below us.

“Because I said hold,” she answered each time. No speech. No appeal to mercy. The order was enough, and she kept giving it.

Denek and I marked the western road with a waist-high rope. Where it forked near the burned hazels, we closed the wrong branch with carts. Drost sorted his diminished soldiers by pace. Those unable to cross wagon ruts rode in blanket-lined grain beds, guarded from wheels, boots and horses. No one laughed. At that scale, a dropped buckle was weight enough to break a foot.

Near sundown, Denek found a collapsed den beside the south fire line. He knelt, put his ear to the earth, and began clearing the entrance with his hands.

“We have to finish the rope,” I said.

“The rope is visible.”

“Not after dark.”

He pulled out another fistful of scorched soil. “Then stop talking.”

I dug beside him until we uncovered a narrow breathing space. Nothing came through it. We went back to the road.

The host began moving when the last rim of sun left the ridge. Their fires stayed cold. Shielded lamps hung inside three wagons, enough for officers to read tally boards but not enough to lay a shadow across the fields. Everyone else followed the rope by touch.

Darkness took away the shape of the army. I heard it instead: boots scuffing, harness rings, wheels easing into ruts, Drost's officers calling intervals. The smallest files made almost no sound. Torma's defenders heard them too. Bows creaked on the wall whenever a horse shied or a cart struck stone, and each time Torma said, “Hold.”

At the burned hazels, one soldier struck flint beside a tangled wheel trace. Three people shouted at once. Drost reached him first and knocked the tinder into mud.

“Use your hands,” he said. “Lift on three.”

There was no threat in it, only the next necessary thing. Six soldiers lifted; the wheel came free. The file moved.

I walked beside the rope until the land rose toward the western boundary. Denek stayed at the fork, repeating the same directions to anyone who lost the line: right hand on rope, carts to the left, ten paces before the cairns. He had spent half his life teaching frightened people how to move through beast country. The purpose had changed. The rules had not.

Restoration began beyond the first cairn. A larger diminished soldier carrying a child-sized comrade cried out as both bodies grew against each other; they had crossed too close together. After that, Drost widened the intervals. Men and women emerged from the dark at mismatched heights, staggered as boots and limbs returned to them, then moved on before the next file arrived. Armor expanded with low clicks of settling plates. Swords stayed sheathed.

Drost crossed near the end. At the boundary he grew from my shoulder height to his full stature in three unsteady steps. He braced one hand on the cairn until the dizziness passed.

“Seventeen?” I asked.

“Fifteen found. Two absent.” His eyes remained on the moving files. “One thousand eight hundred and forty alive at last count.”

“Keep them beyond bow range.”

He gave a tired, irritated motion that might have been agreement or dismissal. It was enough. He went after his army.

By dawn, the last wagon had crossed the ridge. Torma's people collected the abandoned pikes and posted watches around the engines. Drost's host continued west, and its rear guard did not turn before the road bent out of sight.

The valley smelled of wet ash. Three dens had burned. At the south run, Denek found tracks entering the breathing hole we had cleared, though none came out while we watched. One beast was still missing. Crooktail's tracks crossed the fort road twice and ended at the stream.

Torma put the carpenters on the gate and went to argue about grain stores. Denek returned to the collapsed den with a shovel. I carried a new flat stone to the feeding hollow and settled it into the scorched earth.

Near midday, Crooktail appeared beyond the hazels. A band of fur had been rubbed raw around its hindquarters. It watched me tap the stone level with the butt of my knife.

Denek glanced over from the den. “Left edge is high.”

“I know.”

“Then fix it.”

I wedged a chip beneath the right edge. When I looked up, Crooktail had crossed our old twelve-pace measure. It stopped on the near side of the stone, close enough that I could see ash caught in its whiskers.

I set down the eels. Crooktail did not retreat, so neither did I.

stories.title: The Throne Neither of Us Wanted
stories.prompt: You and your older sibling were very anxious if confused when a prophecy was made that one of you would kill your kind father for a throne neither of you particularly wanted. Even stranger, father was entirely unbothered.
stories.body:
# The Throne Neither of Us Wanted

My father was cutting the burned edge from his toast when the rite keeper told us that one of his children would kill him.

The rite keeper had warmed the shallow forecasting dish between her palms until the winter water in it steamed. When she lifted her hands, black grains climbed through the water and fixed themselves against the silver bottom. The dish was only silver. The grains were only grains once her living heat left them. But the pattern they made had not failed in the three hundred years our household had kept records.

My sister read the words first. Her chair struck the tiles behind her.

I read them after.

Before the next turning of the year, one blood-heir will kill the seated king for his throne.

“Does *for* describe motive,” my sister asked, “or result?”

The rite keeper looked tired already. She was accustomed to births, treaties, harvests, ships. Not breakfast with a possible murder between the jam and the butter.

“The pattern does not distinguish.”

“And ‘kill’?”

“The king will die by an heir’s act.”

“Which act?”

“It does not say.”

My sister leaned over the dish as if another clause might be hiding under the rim. She always questioned a disaster until it broke into tasks. At twelve, when I fell through the icehouse roof, she had asked the surgeon which bone, how far, how long, while I screamed at her to stop talking. Later I learned that she had been holding my coat shut around the break.

At breakfast, all I heard was calculation.

“You got to those questions quickly,” I said.

She glanced at me. “Should I have waited?”

Our father slid the charred strip to the edge of his plate. His knife trembled once against the china. Then he reached for the marmalade.

“Father?” I said.

“Mm?”

“Did you hear her?”

“Every word.” He opened the jar, inspected the surface, and pushed it toward my sister. “This is the bitter one. You prefer it.”

She did not take it. “The forecast says one of us will kill you.”

“Yes.”

“For a throne neither of us has asked for.”

“That does make it inconvenient.”

He did not smile. That kept the remark from being a joke, though I wanted it to be one. He spread a careful square of marmalade across the part of his toast that remained.

I could feel my pulse in my gums. “Which of us do you think it is?”

The knife stopped.

“I will not answer that.”

My sister pulled her chair upright. “Because you don’t know?”

“Because the question would do damage whichever name I gave.” He set down the knife. “Your tea is going bitter too.”

This time I heard the tremor in the cup when he lifted it.


The rite keeper let us follow her to the records room because my sister invoked an heir’s right of inspection and I refused to be left alone with our father’s calm.

The room occupied the cold side of the palace, where the windows were narrow and the cabinets smelled of wax, dust, and damp wool. My sister went straight to the succession shelves.

“If we both leave,” I said, “there’s no heir present to act.”

“The line includes blood-heirs abroad.”

“Then we renounce.”

“Renunciation is an act concerning the throne.” She pulled down a ledger. “We don’t know whether it satisfies the forecast.”

“We break the throne.”

The rite keeper was sorting old forecast copies into two stacks. “You may break a chair. You would not break the act already forecast.”

“It is not a chair.”

“It is not a mind either,” she said. “It cannot want you seated. Neither can this morning’s pattern.”

My sister opened the ledger on the nearest table. “Has anyone defeated a reading?”

“People have delayed one. They have misunderstood one. They have committed ugly acts trying to avoid one. Every completed line matched the record in the end.”

“So it compels us.”

“No.” The rite keeper put a finger on the silver dish. The grains had fallen flat now, an illegible grit. “It reports an act. It does not make an heir perform one.”

My sister’s eyes narrowed, not in disbelief but in concentration. She copied the wording onto a scrap, leaving space between every important noun.

“Couldn’t you be frightened like an ordinary person?” I asked.

“I am frightened.”

“You’re making columns.”

“Those are not opposites.”

She turned the ledger toward herself. Tucked beneath its cover was a folded packet in her handwriting. I caught the heading before she covered it with her wrist: *Emergency instruments on death of the sovereign.*

The room went still around me.

“You’ve been here before.”

“I’ve read the current forms.”

“You prepared them.”

“Some of them.”

“Before the prophecy.”

She closed the ledger. “Father has taken medicine four times a day since midsummer. He cancelled the southern circuit. Last week he had the council brought to his room because he could not manage the stairs.”

“He said the old injury was troublesome.”

“Yes.” Her answer was too quick. “And if it became more than troublesome, I wanted us to have options.”

Us. She used that word when she had chosen something for both of us.

I pulled the packet free. There were draft regencies, limits on emergency taxation, a notice preserving my place at the physicians’ college, and a letter to the western survey asking that my sister’s spring commission be held for one year if succession delayed her departure.

I tapped that letter. “Generous of you to postpone your escape.”

“Give me those.”

“You drafted my life after Father, and you were going to mention it when?”

“When there was something to mention.”

“A murdered king might qualify.”

The rite keeper quietly took the silver dish to the far cabinet. My sister reached for the packet, but I held it away.

“If it’s me,” she said, each word clipped clean, “the council will try to keep you here as the next heir. If it’s you, they will try to call your training undignified. I was closing both arguments.”

“You cannot close every argument before the rest of us know we’re in one.”

“Apparently I cannot close this one at all.”

The door opened. One of our father’s attendants stood there with a covered cup.

“The king’s medicine,” she said. “He asked for both of you.”

It was an ordinary sentence. The cup rattled against its saucer in her hands.


We found him in his private room, halfway between the window and the bed.

He was standing only because one hand gripped the curtain cord and the other braced against a table. The physician knelt beside an open case, laying out bottles. Father’s breakfast composure had come apart with his clothes: his collar hung loose, sweat darkened his undershirt, and every breath stopped before it was finished.

My sister dropped the packet. Papers skated under the bed.

“Don’t lift him under the arms,” the physician said. “Support his back. Both of you.”

We obeyed. My sister took most of his weight because she always did; I shoved pillows behind him and knocked one of the medicine bottles over. The physician caught it before it rolled off the table.

“Blue cup,” she said.

The attendant passed it to me.

“Two mouthfuls. Slowly.”

Father drank because I held it to his lips. A thin line escaped into his beard. I wiped it with my sleeve, angry at the medicine, the beard, the hand that had begun to shake in mine.

When his breathing eased, the physician checked his pulse again.

“Tell them,” Father said.

She looked at him. “All of it?”

“There seems little profit in fractions now.”

My sister had gone very quiet.

The physician pulled the chair close to the bed but remained standing. “The scaffold accident last year crushed the king’s chest. The injury was fatal.”

I waited for a second sentence to make the first one sensible.

“He came home,” I said.

“Yes.”

“He recovered.”

“No.”

My father closed his eyes.

The physician continued in the same measured tone she used when telling a patient that a fever had broken or a finger could not be saved. “The coronation working suspended the consequence of the injury while he remained the seated ruler. It gave his body an interval. It did not repair what happened.”

The throne. Not a mind, the rite keeper had said. Not a chooser. A worked mass of black stone beneath a canopy, waiting in a room we visited twice a year for ceremonies we disliked.

“How long?” my sister asked.

“No case in the medical archive passed eighteen months. His pain and weakness have accelerated for six weeks. After this morning, I cannot promise him even another full day of the interval.”

My sister began at once. “Can the working be renewed? Can another living practitioner supply it? Can he resign without transfer? What if the office is divided, or placed in trust, or—”

“No,” the physician said.

The word stopped her.

“A direct heir must freely accept the office,” the physician went on. “The heir sits, takes the ruler’s hand, and speaks acceptance. The support ends when the office passes. What follows is the original injury.”

Kill the seated king for his throne.

I looked at Father. “You knew what the prophecy meant.”

“I suspected.”

“At breakfast, you knew.”

“Yes.”

“And you passed the marmalade.”

His face tightened, whether from pain or shame I could not tell. “It needed passing.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No. It is what I did while I failed to answer.”

My sister stooped to gather her papers. She sorted them on the carpet: regency, tax limits, college, survey. Her hands moved faster than they needed to.

“Why did you hide this?” she asked.

Father looked toward the physician.

“Not her decision,” he said. “Mine. At first I thought there would be time to heal by ordinary means. There wasn’t. Then I thought knowing my pain would force one of you to choose before you could tell duty from fear.”

“So you let us think you were getting better.”

“Yes.”

“You lied.”

“Yes.”

She waited for the gentle qualification he usually found, the comparison to pruning a diseased branch or holding a frightened horse’s bridle. None came.

I asked, “Why aren’t you afraid?”

“I am afraid of hurting you. I am afraid you will punish each other afterward. I am not afraid of the stair happening again.” He opened his eyes and looked at us both. “I remember it. I know what follows. I am tired, and I want this interval to end tonight.”

My sister’s stack slipped sideways. “Then I’ll do it.”

“No,” I said.

She did not look at me. “I am the elder. The instruments already assume—”

“The instruments you wrote.”

“They follow the likely challenge. The council will accept my succession faster. Your college place can be protected by charter. I can appoint—”

“Listen to yourself.”

“I am trying to solve the immediate problem.”

“By becoming the answer before I can speak.”

“Then speak.”

I had nothing. That was the old trick between us: she ran ahead and built the bridge, and I criticized the shape after crossing.

Father pressed a hand against his side. The physician bent to him, but he shook his head.

“Neither of you owes me this,” he said. “And I will not rank your futures to make it easier.”

“You just said you want it tonight,” I said.

“I do.”

“That makes it ours to refuse and yours to suffer.”

“Yes.”

His literal answers were worse than reassurance. They left the choice where it was.


The physician gave us one hour before the next dose, though I suspected she had chosen the interval because a family needed a number to push against.

My sister went to have the throne chamber cleared. I stayed until Father slept, or pretended to. The attendant replaced his damp shirt, and I lifted him while she drew the clean one down his back. We discussed sleeves and buttons. The attendant asked whether he wanted the window latched. The physician counted drops into the blue cup. For ten minutes no one said prophecy, throne, death, or love.

His body said enough. Even asleep, he guarded each breath. When the clock shifted by a quarter hour, he opened his eyes as if the small sound had struck him.

“Is there anything you want?” I asked.

“My grey blanket. The blue one scratches.”

I found the grey blanket in his study, folded across the couch beneath my sister’s travelling coat.

She stood at the writing desk with her spring survey map rolled beside her. The western coast spread across the top sheet: soundings, inlets, a line of proposed beacons. In the corner, she had drawn three alternative routes around a reef. Of course she had.

“The chamber is empty,” she said. “I dismissed the court, guards, musicians, witnesses beyond the rite keeper. We can have the physician close enough without placing her inside. I checked the transfer wording against two reigns and the original stone inscription. There are three clear stops before acceptance. If I take the office, the council can meet at dawn. If I die before appointing—”

“Stop.”

She rolled the map too tightly. It bent near the eastern cape.

“I need to know this is correct.”

“You need to know every consequence except what it costs you.”

“I know what it costs.”

“Say one thing, then.”

“This is not helped by—”

“One thing you wanted next spring.”

She stared at the map.

“The western survey,” I said. “Did you want it?”

“Yes.”

“Was it an escape?”

“Partly.”

“From Father?”

“From being first.” She smoothed the bent corner with her thumb. “First into the council room. First asked when he coughs. First named in every plan. First expected to say it’s manageable.”

Her voice lost its edges. She turned away and tried to tie the map. The cord missed her fingers once, twice.

“I can take it,” she said.

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

“I know.”

Then she had no next option. The silence frightened me more than her columns had.

I laid the grey blanket on the desk. “I keep making you choose, then hating you for choosing.”

“Sometimes you hate me before.”

“Sometimes you make it easy.”

Her breath hitched into something that was not quite laughter. She sat on the couch and put her face in her hands.

I wanted her to tell me what to do. The wanting was so familiar I nearly mistook it for love.

Instead I picked up the blanket.

“I’m taking this to Father.”

She lowered her hands. “Then what?”

“I don’t know yet.”


Father was awake when I returned. I spread the grey blanket over him, tucked it around his feet, and sat beside the bed until the hour ran out.

I thought of the physicians’ college: the basement rooms that smelled of vinegar and boiled linen, the anatomy lectures I had fought to attend, the patients who did not care which chair my ancestors had occupied. I wanted the work. Her western coast did not cancel my basement wards.

I thought of Father’s hand steadying a child’s bowl at breakfast, Father listening to petitions until his ankles swelled, Father quietly removing onions from my plate even after I was old enough to do it myself. He had not become a mechanism when the throne kept his heart moving. His fear, secrecy, pain, and poor decisions were his. So was his request.

If neither of us acted, he would suffer. My sister would keep preparing to act until preparation wore her down into consent. I would keep objecting and leave her hand as the only one visible in the record.

Her regency drafts had protected courses and commissions. None made a place for Father’s next breath.

When the medicine clock rang, I stood.

Father watched me. “Have you decided?”

“I have.”

“Your sister?”

“Has her own decision.”

He nodded once.


The throne chamber looked smaller without the court in it.

No banners hung from the gallery. The candle stands had been pushed against the walls, leaving the black stone chair alone on its low platform. It was broad through the arms and worn pale along the front edge by generations of ceremonial hands. Nothing stirred around it. Nothing called.

My sister waited at the platform with our father’s other arm around her shoulders. She had brought him by the short passage and left her survey coat behind. When she saw me, she searched my face with the same concentration she had given the forecast.

“I’ll do it,” she said.

“I know.”

“There is still time.”

“Yes.”

I went to Father and took his weight from her. For a moment the three of us stood badly tangled at the foot of the throne, adjusting hands and elbows.

“Your foot,” my sister said.

“I know where my foot is.”

“It’s on my hem.”

I moved it. She freed her skirt and guided Father onto the low stool beside the throne. He breathed with his eyes closed until the spasm passed.

Then he said, “The first stop is before you sit.”

My sister stepped between me and the chair. “Why you?”

Not an accusation. She had run out of plans and needed a fact.

“Because I’m choosing it.”

“That isn’t a reason.”

“It’s the one I have.” I touched her sleeve. “Move.”

She caught my wrist. “Not to free me.”

“Not only.”

“Not because you think I can’t bear it.”

“I know you can.”

Her grip tightened. Then she let go and stepped aside.

I sat.

The stone was cold through my clothes. No crown descended. No hidden voice tested my heart. The room remained a room, and my father remained alive on the stool to my left.

“Second stop,” he said. “Before you take my hand.”

I looked at him. “Do you still want this?”

All his gentle evasions were gone. “Yes.”

I reached down. His palm was warm, the fingers dry. He closed them around mine.

The contact ran through the stone beneath me—not a thought or judgment, only a gathered pressure answering two living bodies and the office between them. The pressure held, incomplete.

“Last stop,” Father said. “You may release me and rise.”

My sister knelt in front of him. He set his free hand against her cheek. She covered it with both of hers.

I could hear the physician moving once beyond the closed side door, and courtiers shifting much farther away in the passage. Waiting for a ruler. Waiting for a death. They were the same wait now.

Father looked from my sister to me. “I am ready.”

I held his hand and said, “I accept the office.”

The pressure entered me as heat, then weight: not wisdom, not desire, but every claim the throne made on the body that held it. Beside me, Father drew one startled breath. His shoulders folded.

My sister caught him before he struck the stone.

I left the throne at once and knelt with her. Acceptance had completed the transfer; standing could not undo it.

Father’s hand remained in mine. The physician came through the side door, listened, checked, and after a little while stopped checking.

My sister pressed her forehead to Father’s sleeve. I sat beside them with the throne’s new weight moving quietly through my pulse.


Near midnight, the medicine clock rang in Father’s room.

The court was still waiting beyond the long doors for me to receive them. The physician had taken Father’s body to be washed. My sister and I went instead to stop the clock.

The blue cup stood ready on its saucer. She picked it up, carried it to the basin, and paused.

“Do you want me to speak to them?” she asked.

Once, she would already have drafted the words.

I took the cup from her and rinsed the bitter medicine from it before it could dry around the rim. My hands shook. She held the basin steady, saying nothing.

“Come with me,” I said when the cup was clean.

She set the basin down. “All right.”

We left the medicine clock silent and went to open the doors.

stories.title: There Goes Your Name
stories.prompt: "There goes your name" the fae cooed. "Now, go ahead and pick a new one!" name magic is over rated anyways...
stories.body:
# There Goes Your Name

The first fog came up while we were arguing over a lame ewe.

My sister had the flock's rear, which meant she also had the mud, the stragglers, and every good reason to be cross. I was ahead at the spring, laying the back of my hand against the water to judge whether the cold rain would reach us before dark. Between us, a hundred and six sheep blurred into a long grey drag across the hillside.

"She's putting the bad foot down," my sister called.

The fog carried her voice wide. I could not see her through the sheep, but the name-call tucked my old name into the sound and sent it to me from exactly where she stood: forty paces uphill, a little west, by the scattered thorn. Name-work was useful that way. It was also useful in the way a gate-latch was useful. Nobody wrote songs to a gate-latch.

"Bring her slow," I shouted. "We'll wrap it at the fold."

"And the lamb?"

"With her."

"You counted it?"

I had not. "I can see it."

"You can see fog."

She was fourteen and had recently discovered that accuracy could be sharpened into a household weapon. I found the lamb beside its mother's shoulder, barely more than four trembling legs under a wet fleece, and waved my crook so my sister might glimpse it.

"There. Save your breath for the climb."

"I'm going down."

"Then save it for complaining."

I turned back to the spring and found someone sitting on my pack.

The fae was no taller than my elbow to my fingertips, though its legs hung almost to the ground. It wore no shoes. Pondweed lay slick between its toes, and a spray of rowan berries was braided into hair the brown-green of water seen through peat. It had opened the flap of my pack and was smelling my bread as if deciding which season it belonged to.

"Move," I said.

It lifted its face. Its eyes were pale and round, with no more expression in them than two drops of whey. "You have a lovely sound tied to you. Worn soft at the edges."

My hand went to the horn whistle under my shirt. Father had cut my old name into its flat side when I was seven, two plain syllables in cramped letters because his knife had been too broad for the job.

"That's not for you."

"Oh, the whistle is hard and greasy." The fae wrinkled its nose. "I meant the other thing."

It moved before I did. Two damp fingers touched the hollow of my throat, light as a moth landing. Something snagged—not in my skin, but in the direction of me—and pulled free.

The fae sprang off my pack. It cupped both hands beneath its chin as though carrying a warm egg I could not see.

"There goes your name," the fae cooed. "Now, go ahead and pick a new one!"

"Put it back."

"That one had gone dull. Pick something green. Or round. A name with a bit of rain held in it."

I caught it by the wrist.

Cold ran through my palm. Not winter cold; spring-water cold, so clean it hurt. The fae laughed and folded somehow, its wrist narrowing like a ribbon through my grip. It landed on the stone rim of the spring three steps away, still holding its cupped hands level.

"Give it back," I said.

"But you haven't even tried being without it."

I knew the old name. I knew how Father had said it when I had left a hurdle open, clipping the second syllable because the sheep were already in the beans. I knew my sister stretched the first when she wanted me to answer across weather. In the flock ledger, my name stood beside the winter feed accounts and the note about the north wall. It was mine in all the usual ways.

"I have work."

The fae lowered one hand to trail its fingers in the spring. The other remained closed. "Work has so many noises. Scuff, huff, clack, tear. A name gives only one."

Behind me, the dog gave one sharp bark.

The flock had begun to bunch. Fog thickened across the slope, swallowing the thorn and then the backs of the last sheep. I put two fingers to my mouth and whistled the dog round to the west. It knew that signal. The sheep turned downhill, shoulder pressing shoulder, wool brushing with a sound like rain in dry grass.

"You," I said to the fae. "Stay there."

It smiled. "Which you?"

I left it at the spring because the lame ewe was moving and my sister had sense enough to follow.

For perhaps five minutes, that was true.

Then the lame ewe veered downhill past the old sheepfold, her lamb at her shoulder. The dog went after them. I stepped into the open side of the fold, driving the leaders around the dry-stone wall, and the fog closed behind them so neatly it seemed to cut the flock in two. Bells knocked. Hooves scraped. I whistled twice for my sister to tighten the rear.

No whistle came back.

I called her by her name. The call went to her, wherever she was, but no answer came back.

"That's poor," said the fae from the wall above me. "Throwing a voice without a string."

"What did you do?"

It opened its palm for a moment. I saw no written word, no glowing mark, only the faint bend of light above its skin, as if sun lay under moving water. Then its fingers closed again.

My sister called my old name.

Her voice came from the wall where the fae sat.

I looked up so fast the rim of my hood struck my cheek. The fae tipped its head, listening to the call arrive. It breathed across its fist and turned its wrist. My sister's second call slid left with that motion and faded toward the upper path.

"Stop that."

"I carry it. That is where it goes."

"You are carrying it. You are turning her voice."

"Yes."

No shame. No threat, either. It said yes as my sister might say the ewe had four feet. I climbed the loose outer face of the wall and reached for it. The fae hopped down inside the fold, brushing past the damp noses of three ewes. They flinched because it touched them, not because they knew what it was.

My sister called again. The fae ran toward the uphill gap, cooing the two syllables back to itself—not answering, only savoring their shape. The call followed it.

I ran after.

The upper path climbed between heather and broken stone. It was the wrong road for the lower pasture, the wrong road for a lame ewe, and the wrong road under a sky holding that much rain. I knew all three facts. I also heard my sister's breath behind every call bent uphill, and knowledge became a poor thin thing beside it.

The fae stayed just ahead. Now and then I saw rowan-red beads in the fog. It paused on a boulder, both hands closed around what it had taken, and offered, "You could be called moss. You step like moss trying not to be a boot."

"How far can she be?"

"From what?"

"From the name-call."

"Near enough to want you."

"A mile? Two?"

It considered. "Not two. Two has too much road in it."

"Can she hear me?"

"If you make a noise."

I blew the horn whistle: one long note, two short, our ordinary recall. The sound flattened in the fog, directionless but loud. I waited.

Nothing answered.

The fae dangled from the boulder by its knees. "Try a softer name next. This one has been said across too many fields."

I pulled the whistle from its thong and held the carved side toward it. "My father gave me this name."

"Your father put scratches on bone."

"Horn."

"Horn, then. It smells of your neck."

"He gave me the word before he carved it."

The fae swung itself upright. "You still have the word. Look. Say it to yourself."

I did, silently. Every sound remained where memory kept it. That did not make the fae's theft small.

"He is dead," I said. "I can't ask him for another."

The fae leaned close enough that I smelled crushed mint and sheep dung on its breath. "Dead people leave old sounds. This one drags at the end. Can't you feel it?"

Below us, the dog barked twice.

I turned. Its shape was only a dark patch in the fog, down by the fold. It stood facing downhill, ears pricked away from me.

The fae had followed my gaze. "It doesn't know your new sound."

"It doesn't need one."

On the path at my feet, every hoofprint pointed down.

Not many: the narrow print of the lame ewe, the two neat punches of the lamb, and my sister's boot heel smeared through the edge of both. A strand of wet wool clung to a low juniper on the downslope side. There were no fresh marks continuing uphill except mine.

My sister called again. Her voice came from behind me.

The fae stood behind me.

This time I watched it work. It raised its closed hand as she called and drew the sound toward itself with a long inhalation, pleased as a child smelling cakes. The old name had not led me anywhere. The fae had.

"You've been running," I said.

It smiled. "So have you."

I dropped to one knee beside the prints. Rain had not yet filled them. The lame ewe was setting the bad hind hoof along its outer edge, as she had in the morning. My sister had kept her on the softer ground until the juniper. Beyond it, the slope broke toward the scree channel.

The dog whined.

"Go find," I told it, and gave my sister's ordinary hand-signal: palm low, two fingers forward. No magic in that. Training, meat scraps, years.

The dog vanished downhill.

The fae skipped beside me when I followed. "Moss is still available. Or milkcap. You have the look of something found under a leaf."

"Do you have to answer when she calls?"

"I don't answer. I turn it."

"Do you have to turn it?"

The fae's toes tested a slick stone and withdrew. "No."

"Then don't."

"But the way she worries your old sound is lovely."

I stopped so sharply it nearly walked into me. "She's on bad ground with a lame ewe. If you send me wrong again, she may fall."

For once, the fae did not fill the space. Rain ticked in the heather. A sheep coughed somewhere inside the fold.

Then the fae said, almost complaining, "I didn't tell her to stand there."

"No. You only kept me from finding her."

It rubbed its closed fist with the thumb of its other hand. "People usually chase what I take."

"I did."

"You stopped."

A thin whistle rose below us, one long note. It broke halfway through the second, ended in a breathy crack, then did not come again.

My sister's reed whistle. She had mended the mouthpiece twice with thread and wax and claimed it would last the winter. It had not lasted the afternoon.

The dog barked from the same direction.

I went down.

The fae followed without speaking. It came upright now, using hands as well as feet on the wet rock, still keeping the fist with my old name lifted away from every scrape. The slope steepened below the juniper. Grey stones shifted under brown grass, all of it slick as fat. I found where the ewe had slid: four furrows, a tuft of belly wool, blood no larger than a berry on one sharp edge.

"Stay high," my sister shouted. No name this time. Her voice came from below and a little east, plain direction carried by the wind when it happened to be kind. "The middle's loose."

"Can you move?"

"I can. She can't. Lamb's here too."

"Anything broken?"

"Whistle. Maybe my backside."

"That will heal your manners."

"Come say that down here."

There she was: crouched on a shelf of stone scarcely wide enough for her boots, one arm braced behind the lame ewe's neck. The lamb was wedged between her knees, shivering but upright. The dog stood on a firmer lip below, looking up and refusing to climb the shifting fan between us.

My sister had mud to one eyebrow and the furious, frightened look she got when fear seemed an accusation against her competence.

"Don't move the ewe," I said.

"Hadn't planned to throw her."

"I need the rope."

"You have it."

I reached for the coil at my belt and found an empty hook.

She closed her eyes. "You left it on the gate."

"I did."

"You told me to mind the gate."

"Yes."

"I was minding a sheep."

"Keep doing that."

The fae crouched above the scree, peering at my sister. "She's red under the mud. Like a rowan fruit dropped in broth."

My sister stared at it. "Is that what stole your name?"

"Yes."

"Ugly little midden-pip. Give it back."

The fae drew itself up. "I am not ugly."

"Then stand somewhere useful."

I sent the dog back with the hand-signal for the fold. It hesitated, glanced at my sister, and went when I repeated it. While we waited, I tested the slope with the crook. The middle ran at a touch. The safer line curved east across a narrow band of grass, down to the dog's ledge, then back under my sister's shelf. We would need the rope for the ewe. We would need my sister to move first.

"The lamb goes inside your coat," I told her. "Feet down."

"It kicks."

"So do you."

"Not when folded."

She managed it. The lamb disappeared against her belly, its nose poking between two buttons. She looked absurdly pregnant and entirely unable to laugh about it.

"Left foot to the grass," I said. "Not the grey stone."

"It's all grey."

"The one with the black edge. Reach past it."

She shifted. Pebbles ran from under her boot. The ewe lurched against her hip.

"Wait," I said.

"I'm waiting."

"You're moving."

"The sheep is moving."

Her sentences came apart with her breath. Mine had shortened until every word seemed to have a job and resent the others.

The fae watched the stones move. "They sound like dry seeds in a pod."

Neither of us answered.

The dog returned dragging the lambing rope by one loop. It had caught twice on heather and collected half the hillside. I climbed down to take it, tied one end around my waist, and threw the cleanest loop toward my sister. The first fell short. The second struck her shoulder.

"Under your arms," I said.

"Ewe first."

"You first."

"If she goes, she takes me."

That was true. She threaded the rope behind the ewe's forelegs instead, working one-handed around the lamb beneath her coat. I braced on the lower ledge and took the weight while she urged the ewe across. The animal placed its sound hoof, dragged the sore one, and tried to turn back. The dog dropped flat where she could see it. My sister pressed her shoulder to the ewe's rump.

"Easy," she said. "No, not there. Here. That's grass. Put your stupid foot on it."

The ewe listened to pressure, footing, and the dog's stillness. She did not need a name. She reached my ledge trembling. I lowered her to the dog, who stood and kept her from turning uphill.

My sister worked the loop free of the ewe and passed it under her own arms. Then she crossed with the lamb. Halfway, the black-edged stone rolled. Her left foot went out.

She did not call my name. She said, "Rope!"

I dropped my weight backward. The line snapped tight under her arms. She struck the slope on one knee, showering us both with shale, but her right boot found the grass band. I hauled while she crawled. The lamb bleated once from inside her coat, offended but alive.

When she reached me, she pushed the lamb into my hands and sat down hard.

"You took your time," she said.

"I went uphill."

"Why?"

I looked at the fae. It had come down to the shelf we had left and was tracing the ewe's blood-speck on the stone with one damp finger.

"Because it moved the call," I said.

My sister wiped mud from her eyebrow and made the smear worse. "You always say calls make people lazy."

"I do."

"You were right, then. That's annoying."

"Get up."

She got up.

We brought the ewe and lamb back by the long lower curve. The rain arrived properly, needling the backs of our hands and turning the dog's coat black. Behind the fold wall, the flock had divided itself according to no scheme useful to us: yearlings in the corner meant for ewes, two rams nosing the broken hurdle, and one lamb perched on the feed stone as if supervising.

My sister took the far wall. "Let's see where the old one sends me now."

She called my old name. Her voice came from the fae under its dock leaf instead of from her.

"Still broken," she said.

"Mine, not yours."

The fae sat on the wall under a dock leaf, keeping one fist closed. "Broken is harsh. Empty has more room in it."

"Give back the old one," my sister said.

"No."

"Why not?"

"I like how it has been used."

My sister took one step toward the wall. I caught the back of her coat.

"Leave it," I said.

"I'm not leaving it. I'm knocking it into the nettles."

"We have a lame ewe, a wet lamb, and a gate that won't hold."

"Also that."

"The gate first."

She gave the fae a look that promised future nettles and went to lift the dropped hurdle. I stood in the rain with Father's whistle against my chest and listened to the flock shove and mutter. My old name was not empty of use. It belonged to his voice, to my sister's, to the cut letters under my thumb. The fae could keep carrying the bent call for now. It could not take those.

But my sister still needed a sound that would reach me straight when the weather hid us.

At the spring, long pale sedge bent under the rain and rose when each gust passed. We cut it every winter for bedding. Its roots held the black edge of the bank where sheep would otherwise punch through.

Nothing truer than that. Something useful.

I went to the fold entrance where my sister could see me. "I'll use Sedge."

She stopped with the hurdle against her shoulder. "You will?"

"For calling."

"All right."

"Say it back. Mean me."

Her face tightened with concentration. She had known me all her life, which did not prevent her from doing things badly on principle. This she did carefully.

"Sedge," she called.

The sound reached me from her place at the far side of the fold. Not louder. Not sweetened. It came through rain and milling sheep with its direction clean inside it.

The fae opened both hands. A bend of light remained above the palm that held my old name; the other palm was bare. It laughed, delighted rather than defeated.

"One weather-stem," it said. "And one old bell-sound."

"Are you keeping the old one?" I asked.

It tucked its closed fist beneath its chin. "For a while."

Then it dropped from the wall into the fog. Rowan berries flashed once and were gone.

My sister set the hurdle back into its sockets. "Sedge."

"What?"

"Nothing. Trying it."

"Try it while you sort the yearlings."

She went left. I went right. The dog brought the first six through the narrow gate, and for several minutes there were only wet backs, reaching hands, the knock of wood, and my sister telling a ram exactly what she thought of its mother.

Then her voice found me cleanly from behind the flock.

"Sedge, your side!"

I turned in time to block the lame ewe from following the yearlings through. Her lamb squeezed under my arm. My sister laughed once, breathless, and shoved the hurdle closed.

"Wrap that foot," she said. "Rain's getting in."

I reached for the wool bandage in my pack. "Count the lambs first."

"I already did."

"How many?"

She held up both muddy hands because she knew I hated waiting while she counted on her fingers. The dog shook rain across my legs. Somewhere beyond the wall, the fae made a small pleased sound, or perhaps it was only water slipping under the stones.

My sister got to one hundred and six. We started again to make sure.

stories.title: The Vacant Throne
stories.prompt: Fifteen years ago, the human king and the demon queen fought a legendary battle that resulted in the king's death. The throne remained vacant until a half-demon child appeared bearing the royal sword.
stories.body:
# The Vacant Throne

The keep gate was already lifting when Vumo reached it.

They came at a stumbling run through the evening market, one hand clamped over the wrapped hilt above their shoulder, the other holding the scabbard clear of the stones. The sword was nearly as long as they were tall. Its iron tip had beaten a dark rhythm against every mile from the eastern ridge, and Vumo's palm had gone numb before noon.

"Wait," they called. "I have to see Veldan."
