“A hole is a hole when the beam breaks.”

“Cut me the two sisters. I shore one bay and open no more than that. If the timber gives us no answer, we dismantle.”

“You dismantle.” He folded the board once, precise as a refusal. “My saw stays out of it.”

Agnes set a peg against one bore and tapped twice with her mallet.

From under the floor came two faint knocks. A pause followed, long enough for Silas to turn toward the door. Then came a third.

He unfolded the board.

* * *

The wet joist betrayed the route. Its upper face looked sound, but Agnes's awl sank to the haft beside a black iron nail. Rather than skin it over, she numbered the floorboards in chalk and lifted them from the gallery wall toward the middle of the room.

Beneath the ordinary boards lay an older sprung floor of elm laths. Bits of blue glazing glittered in the dust. A border of green-and-white tile survived under the later skirting, and in the dead spaces Agnes found three stamped dance tokens, a bone button, and enough bent pins to furnish a dozen lost sleeves. Whoever had built the grand room had spent money on light, color, and a floor gentle under moving feet.

They had also patched, generation after generation, around the same hollow oak dowels.

The dowels descended through the wall frame beside a copper gutter. Unlike the green metal around it, the gutter's inner lip shone where repeated pouring had worn it smooth. It sloped toward the swollen cellar door and vanished through older masonry.

“What did they pour?” Agnes asked.

“Cellars take ale.” Silas kept his eyes on the lifted boards.

“Ale goes down by cask and comes up by jug. It doesn't need a serving gutter inside a wall.”

He answered by fetching the pry bar.

They freed the cellar door a fraction at a time. Beyond it, stone steps fell into air warmer than the hall. Agnes's lamp showed a cracked drain, clay pipes, and a copper grille furred shut with verdigris. At the back, built into stonework older than any wall above, lay the curved shell of an enormous oak cask. Tool marks on it were broad and shallow, unlike the crisp later mortises that accommodated its shape. Three floors had been raised around it. None had disturbed it.

The smell was not rot. It was warm malt after rain.

Pale cords webbed the cask's broken staves and entered the hollow dowels overhead. They withdrew from Agnes's lamp, not all at once but in tightening ripples. Among them moved amber mites, grain-small and glossy. Some carried damp pulp toward a pale cluster of brood. Along one charred stave, old fungal tissue had ridged over a burn.

“The Underbreath,” Silas said behind her.

Agnes lowered the lamp. “You know it.”

“Knew the name. A cellar pest. Old folk blamed it for sour barrels.”

“Old folk built it a copper trough.”

“Old folk built many foolish things.”

One loose gallery peg stood proud above them. A fresh cord entered its dowel. As Agnes watched, the cord tightened and the oak grain drew fractionally closed. Upstairs, the peg settled by the thickness of a shaving.

The cord was fine as sewing thread. Its flesh could not by ordinary leverage have closed a handspan of old oak, much less shifted a peg upstairs. Yet its contraction had travelled through the dowel, and the old joinery had carried the impossible force. The life below supplied what the cask and pipe could only route.

Agnes shaded a dry margin with her hand, fed it a spoonful of water, and waited. Fresh translucent tips emerged along the damaged edge. A mite returned with pulp. Another followed.

“You wanted the cellar opened,” Silas said. “Now you've seen why it was shut.”

“I've seen why someone wanted me to think shutting it was sensible.”

She refused his jar of fumigating bitter. Instead she set shallow dishes of watered malt, opened three temporary vent runs, and marked every peg above with a hairline of chalk. Silas watched her work without helping.

“If that brings the gallery down?” he asked.

“Then I learn before there are customers under it.”

“And if it brings something else?”

Agnes looked at the brood gathered in the cask's damp seam. “Then you may try answering the question you keep stepping around.”

* * *

The drain had been laid with a mean little rise just before the outer wall. Agnes lifted two stones, reset the clay channel on packed lime and gravel, and gave the water a clean fall. She scraped the copper grille open and hinged it outward. Over the cask's split stave she fitted an oak sleeve with breathing gaps instead of packing the crack with mortar.

Only then did she test the structure.

She hung one measured sandbag from a colonized peg and gave two taps. Two taps returned through the dowel. That proved response, perhaps only habit. She needed a choice the old system had not taught.

From the cask she laid three covered channels. One held fresh air from the opened grille. One held watered malt. The third followed a smoke-stained clay branch toward the gallery wall; she placed malt there too, so food and safety would not point the same way.

The pale cords nosed first toward both dishes. At the bitter soot they recoiled. Mites left the nearer food untouched and began carrying brood toward the fresh-air channel. Agnes blocked that channel with a tile.

The sandbag peg released.

It dropped half an inch into its mortise, and the bag touched the floor. The cords did not take the offered food. They spread along the cask seam, found the edge of her tile, and sent one bright thread past it toward the copper grille.

Not speech. Not proof of a mind shaped like hers. But it was no echo either. Faced with three poor choices, the colony had refused two, protected its young, and surrendered a load.

Agnes removed the tile at once.

She traced the smoke branch upward. Behind the hearth, the flue divided through a shutter and a leather-bellows throat she had already rebuilt from fragments because its curve matched the earliest plaster. Bitter black lay only in the branches leading to structural bays. On one exposed beam, pale cords had grown around old burns and sealed them with scar tissue.

The wall tallies changed too. Early accounts paired malt measures with feast nights. Later hands bought more bitter fuel, recorded less feed, and demanded larger crowds from the same thin joists. That showed a change in practice, not what the first builders had intended. The oldest truth remained below the oldest readable wall.

Silas arrived near dusk and found Agnes scrubbing SAVE from the fascia. Beneath it she wrote, SUPPORT WITHOUT IT.

“That's a dear sentence,” he said.

“Less dear than a funeral.”

“You'll lose half the room.”

“I'll lose the part that doesn't know how to stand.” She held out a soot-black flue tile. “Who taught them to drive it with this?”

Silas looked past her to the chalked plan. “Put your roof on before the storm. Questions keep better than lime.”

He left the tile in her hand.

The deed still hung above the counter. It conveyed beams, stone, fixtures, and land by boundary. Nothing written there could turn the small lives below into stock. Agnes took up her rule and began drawing posts.

* * *

The storm arrived a day earlier than the carter's forecast. Wind rammed rain beneath the temporary roof and pressed smoke down the chimney. Agnes smelled the bitter residue before she heard the gallery move.

The rebuilt bellows shutter clapped open.

Smoke drove through the old clay branches into the hollow dowels. Beneath the floor, the Underbreath contracted in flight. Its force tightened the colonized oak, drew two pegs home, and lifted the bowed gallery almost level.

For one terrible moment the grand room returned. Gold brackets aligned. The rail rose straight. Agnes could see the lamps, the musicians on the speaking step, the crowd above moving as one body.

Then a rotten mortise split with the report of an axe.

Silas came through the main door carrying a wrapped book under his coat. “You've set the draw back.”

“I set it to the earliest profile.” Agnes braced a second prop beneath the inner beam. “The front bay is taking more than its share. Help me shore it.”

“Earliest you could see.” He put the book on the counter and opened it to a page of flue diagrams. “My forebear kept this. My family kept it after.”

The sketched branches matched the ones in the wall. Late entries grew meaner: *brood dead at east stave*; *feed shortened*; *drive the Underbreath hard for festival*. Beside one blot, a hand had drawn the same bellows shutter Agnes had restored.

“You had this while I was opening the floor?”

“I wanted the place shut.”

“You wanted the evidence shut.”

The gallery lurched. A peg sprang across the room and struck the hearth. Silas flinched, then caught the prop Agnes shoved at him.

“Blame me when the roof is holding,” he said.

Closing the shutter would stop new smoke. It would not cool the oak already hot, open a path for the colony, or support the frame when panicked cords let go. The outer bay had begun to peel away from the wall. If it fell uncontrolled, it would wrench the sound inner beam off its shores.

Agnes looked once at the gilded rail. Nearly all her savings, made visible.

“We're not shoring the front,” she said. “We're cutting it free.”

* * *

The safe door was behind them. The smoking hearth stood to their right. Across the room, beyond the bowed gallery, the cellar steps led to the drain and the copper grille. Agnes set out the order before fear could disorder it.

“Inner beam first. Both shores under sound heartwood. Then the grille full open. Then I break the shutter out.”

Silas looked up at the carved outer bay. “We can stand two more props under that rail.”

“On the sprung floor? It will punch through and trap us beneath it.” Agnes drove her rule into the scarf line where the decorated cantilever joined the inner beam. “This joint is already half opened. We support here, cut here, and wedge the dead bay outward.”

“That's the room you bought.”

“It's the room that was bought before.”

There was no time to make the sentence better. Another contraction jerked the rail upward and showered them with lime.

They raised the independent shores. Agnes held each plumb while Silas struck the wedges. The first seated under the inner beam with a clean knock. The second skidded on wet flagstone; she kicked grit beneath its sole and made him drive again.

“Three blows,” she said. “No more. One. Two. Three.”

The inner beam settled onto honest timber.

Silas ran for the cellar. Agnes crossed to the hearth, keeping outside the gallery's fall line. She hooked her pry bar behind the shutter she had so carefully fitted, levered until the new screws tore from old brick, and ripped the whole bellows throat into the ashes. Smoke burst into the hall, then thinned as the pressure found the open fireplace instead of the clay branches.

From below came the clang of copper and Silas shouting, “Grille's open!”

Cool wet air entered at floor level. It carried the smell of rain on nettles. Through a gap beside the dance floor, Agnes saw the pale cords still drawn taut, their edges gone translucent with heat. They did not release. Familiar smoke had taught flight into the beams too well.

She laid the long saw into the old scarf joint.

The teeth caught gilding first, then oak. Each pull cost her a month's rent, ten chairs, another strip of gallery she would never be able to claim as original. Sawdust fell red-brown through the gold. Above her, the outer bay shuddered as the Underbreath tightened; behind her, the independent posts held the inner beam without complaint.

Silas returned dripping. “Let me take the saw.”

“Take the wedge. When I reach the hollow, knock it outward.”

“The carving could be braced after.”

Agnes pointed with the saw handle. The scarf had split past its shoulder; rot ran through the decorated face; the colonized dowel bound the dying bay to the sound frame. “If we keep that, we keep the smoke route and the false load. The whole piece goes.”

He put the maul to the wedge.

Agnes cut. The saw passed solid grain, soft rot, then the hollow dowel. Warm, bitter air hissed from it. Beneath the floor, pale growth streamed toward the damp channel. Amber mites crowded the open route. A fresh cord touched the copper lip.

The load changed.

“Now,” Agnes said.

Silas struck.

For an instant the Underbreath pulled against the old command. The gallery rose a finger's width. Then the colonized peg slid free. Cords withdrew from the severed dowel in a pale rush, abandoning the outer bay.

The carved rail tipped away from them. It struck the cleared, roped floor in one vast cracking blow. Blue-glass fragments leapt from the dust. Agnes felt the impact through her boots, but the inner beam remained on its new posts. The roof did not follow.

Neither of them spoke until the last small piece of plaster had fallen.

In the cellar, the cask-shell was scorched but damp. Fresh cords filled its shaded seam and reached along the open grille; none returned to the separated gallery stump. The colony had stayed where it had a way to leave. That was a choice for tonight, not a promise Agnes could nail in place.

Upstairs, the deed had come loose from its pin. She picked it out of the dust, folded it, and put it in her pocket.

* * *

By the harvest gathering, the hall carried itself.

Two new oak posts stood where the gallery's front bay had been. Agnes had left them visible, their wedges and tool marks plain. She conserved the surviving madder procession and one jagged end of gilded rail, but she did not paint in the missing bodies or pretend the gallery still wrapped three walls. The smaller room held fewer tables. It also held no concealed load.

Beside the cellar door hung a notice describing the cask-shell, the living colony, the smoke damage, and the limits of what the records proved. The cellar was occupied habitat, not storage and not entertainment. The copper grille remained open. Water and malt went down whether or not any peg ever moved again.

Silas inspected both posts before he took off his coat. He had brought sound oak at his own cost and placed the maintenance book beneath the notice in a glass-fronted box. Agnes had thanked him for the timber. The notice still said how long the book had been kept back.

“Six tables lost,” he said.

“Five. I made the counter narrower.”

He read the notice again. “People will ask to see below.”

“They may ask.”

Silas tested the cellar latch, found it locked, and nodded toward the doors. “They're waiting in the rain.”

Together they opened the Hollow Cask.

Neighbors filled the speaking step and the floor. Musicians tuned where the dancers had once worn elm smooth. Agnes drew the first mug, listening despite herself for strain in the posts. There was none.

Music began. Warm barley air rose through the open copper grille, and one small, voluntary tremor dimpled the foam.

stories.title: The Strength of Ten
stories.prompt: Your kingdom is defenseless, and to secure an army, you, the prince, are promised in marriage to one of the daughters of the King of the North, a brutal warrior known for having the strength of 10 men.
stories.body:
# The Strength of Ten

The courier caught Prince Lysander beneath Harrowfast's gatehouse, before he could offer the gold wedding chain to the steward waiting on the steps.

Snow had packed white in the courier's eyebrows. His horse stood with its head down between six others, all seven animals trembling from the Frostroad. Lysander's own six escorts looked scarcely better.

"Greyglass is lost," the courier said. "The marshal sold the gate. Most of the four hundred border guards were taken in their beds. The rest came south without weapons."

Lysander felt the chain's square links through his glove. "How far is the Black Reed train?"

"A hundred and five miles from Ninepin. Six days, if the thaw doesn't speed them." The courier glanced at the northern steward and abandoned deference. "We have a hundred and eighty city watch and seventy riders. No seasonal companies. No border line. Come home."

Home had granaries worth an invasion, river locks worth a dynasty, and no army because Lysander had sent thirteen hundred hungry soldiers back to their farms before autumn. He had called that mercy. Later, when the Greyglass warnings came, he had called Redwater merely outnumbered.

"Ride back," he said. "Empty the three villages along Ninepin. Put every sluice worker under the watch. Assemble one hundred and twenty grain carts with fodder enough to reach the day-four post on the Frostroad."

"From what depot?"

"The river stores. Break my seals."

The courier's mouth tightened. It was not enough, but it was work that might be done. He mounted again.

Lysander gave the wedding chain to no one. He carried it into King Gorm's hall himself, resolved to marry whichever of Gorm's three grown daughters the king required.

* * *

An iron-banded oak table divided Gorm's hall. It was wide enough for maps, a winter feast, or a body laid out for judgment. The king of the North sat beyond it in shirtsleeves despite the cold, thick wrists bare, his old scar-lattice showing pale above his collar.

"Three thousand northerners," Gorm said. "At Ninepin before the reeds turn green."

A road clerk beside the wall cleared his throat. "Sixteen hundred can be spared without opening the northern passes."

Gorm held out one hand. The clerk went still, then removed the copper ration badge from his neck and laid it in the king's palm.

"Outer arch," Gorm told him. "Until the last bell. No brazier. Perhaps cold will improve your arithmetic."

The clerk bowed and left without his cloak. No one watched him go except Lysander.

Gorm smiled again. "Prince Lysander, my second daughter is thirty-two, unmarried, and more useful than many sons. You will have Princess Sigrun. Redwater will have my strength and my host."

The side door opened before Lysander could answer. Princess Sigrun came in carrying two ledgers and a roll of road maps under one arm. She wore a marshal's grey coat, damp at the shoulders, and had grain dust on one cuff.

"You will not have three thousand," she said. "And I will not marry him."

At thirty, Lysander had crossed one hundred and forty miles rehearsing surrender. "Princess Sigrun, I understand what is required. I accept the match."

Her eyes settled on him. "Did you come here to request my answer, or to carry it?"

The courtesy he had prepared offered no safe clause. "I came for an army."

"There is one honest quantity."

Gorm laughed. "At Rimegate they mistook counting for command too. They built a coal barricade across my road. Ten men could not shift it."

He stood and braced both hands beneath the table's edge.

The old stories said a living field-healer had laid those scar paths into him after a spear wound, decades ago, and that Gorm had learned to drive his own heat and strength through them in a single, ruinous effort. Lysander had assumed the strength of ten men was northern embroidery.

Gorm drew one measured breath. The scars along his throat darkened.

On the first heartbeat, the table groaned. On the second, its feet tore splinters from the floor. By the sixth, Gorm had dragged the massive thing sideways across the main doors. The iron bands struck stone. Anyone who left now would need his leave to pass through the private rooms behind him.

"Then I broke Rimegate," he said. "They yielded before dark."

His voice held, but one hand shook when he released the oak. A servant hurried forward with furs. Another brought heated stones and broth. Gorm lowered himself into his chair with the careful stiffness of a wounded man.

Sigrun did not look away from her father. "And you withheld their household coal until they did."

She placed an unsigned route ledger on the table he had moved. Six depot seals marked its first page. Twelve blank spaces waited beneath them.

"You may call troops," she said. "You may shut doors. But the keepers will not release grain, the remount masters will not open their barns, and the captains will not take the Frostroad until my ledger matches theirs. The seven reeves can replace me if you remove me. Their notices have ten days of road between them."

Gorm's face had gone grey beneath its weathered red. He had the strength of ten haulers for six heartbeats. Redwater had six days.

For the first time, Lysander saw that the bride and the army had never been one transaction.

* * *

While Gorm withdrew to be warmed, Sigrun took Lysander to the map room. On the way she stopped at the outer arch, dismissed the shivering clerk in the name of her office, and fastened the copper badge back around his neck.

Then she began counting what Lysander had tried not to name.

"Black Reed foot?"

"About forty-five hundred. Six hundred horse. Engineers and siege wagons."

"Your standing force?"

"Four hundred at Greyglass."

"No. Your standing force now."

The map between them showed Reedmarsh as a wash of green ink with one hard black line through it. "A hundred and eighty watch. Seventy couriers."

"Seasonal companies?"

"Released."

"Your letter said delayed."

"I released them early. There was not enough grain for soldiers and households both."

Sigrun waited.

"I chose the households," he said. "Then I discounted the warnings from Greyglass because calling the companies back would have admitted that the choice left us open."

She turned to a clean sheet. No comfort, no accusation. Only a sharper quill.

Three thousand soldiers, she showed him, would consume Redwater's promised carts before the fourth day and strip Harrowfast's passes. Sixteen hundred could cross in five days if six depots released grain, grease, socks, traces, and remounts in sequence. Eight hundred shield-spears. Four hundred bows. Two hundred and fifty pioneers. One hundred and fifty scouts. Two hundred and forty drivers, healers, smiths, and depot workers would sustain them.

"No foraging," she said. "If your carts fail, I turn the columns north."

"Agreed."

"I command until Black Reed retreats beyond Greyglass or twenty days pass. You command your watch and workers. Three captain-representatives may refuse pillage, pursuit beyond the border, or abandonment of Ninepin."

Lysander looked at the causeway. One firm road across thawing marsh, narrow enough to make five thousand less useful. "Evacuate the villages. Open both culverts when the train commits. Anchor wagons in the center."

"Harrowfast iron travels through your locks," Sigrun said. "If Black Reed takes the capital, our spring trade pays whatever tariff it names. This is not charity."

"If your sluice workers are there." Her quill moved. "Harrowfast supplies three days. Redwater supplies the carts and fodder. One third of the river-lock tolls for seven years goes to wages, injured households, roads, and the three displaced villages."

Seven years. His council would call it northern occupation written in columns.

"And a public tribunal," Sigrun said. "You testify about the demobilization, Greyglass, and the letter you sent us. If Redwater's lawful council finds you broke your office, you accept its decision on the succession."

There it was. The cost that could not be worn nobly around his neck.

"A wedding after the campaign might make these terms acceptable to your father," Lysander said. "When there is time to decide it freely."

Sigrun set down the quill.

He heard what he had done: taken her no, dressed it in a later season, and offered it back as compromise.

"Strike that," he said. "No wedding."

She drew a line through the blank marriage clause. "The compact can work without one. Can you?"

He stared at the tribunal provision. He had been ready to give his body to a stranger and remain prince. This asked him to give Redwater facts it might use to remove him.

"I don't know," he said.

"Find out before the road freezes without us."

* * *

A second Redwater courier arrived at dusk with his horse spent beneath him. Black Reed's siege wagons had turned onto the south road. The northern columns had to leave before dawn.

Sigrun read the compact aloud in Gorm's hall. The king sat under three furs, a hot stone against his ribs. His right hand still trembled. The table remained jammed across the doors.

"I remove you as road-marshal," he said.

Sigrun laid seven copied notices beside the route ledger, each bearing spaces for a reeve's mark. "Then no keeper opens a depot until the reeves appoint another marshal. The captains have been told. Ten days, if every road stays open."

"I have other daughters." Gorm looked at Lysander. "My eldest is grown and less enamored of account books. Take her."

Lysander thought of a woman not in the room being fitted to the empty clause. "No."

Gorm's gaze hardened. "My youngest, then. All three know their duty."

"I will not ask either of them to purchase soldiers for me. Princess Sigrun said no. The marriage promise ends there."

"Then take eight hundred of my household spears. Marry Sigrun tonight, and the Redwater tolls remain mine after seven years."

Sigrun tapped the force count. "Eight hundred cannot hold Ninepin and the depots will not feed an unauthorized levy."

The king rounded on her. "You would let his kingdom fall to spite me?"

"I have sixteen hundred people harnessing sleds while you ask which daughter will make you richest. Sign the call, or they unharness."

Gorm began a tale about Rimegate. His voice faltered when he reached for the table and his shaking fingers could not close on its edge.

Lysander unhooked the wedding chain. "My kingdom is not merely outnumbered," he said, loudly enough for the captains and clerks along the walls. "It is defenseless. I dismissed thirteen hundred soldiers, then concealed what I had done."

The words did not make him lighter. Good.

He signed the compact beneath Sigrun's name. He surrendered command of the northern host, one third of the river tolls for seven years, and any certainty that the tribunal would leave him heir. Then he laid the chain across the accounts.

"Weigh this into the casualty fund."

Sigrun examined the heavy clasp. "The gold, yes. The promise, no."

She cut the chain from its clasp with the clerk's shears. The twelve captains marked the route ledger. Three representatives countersigned the limits. At last Gorm pressed his seal into the levy call.

"You came north for the strength of ten men," he told Lysander, recovering enough breath for grandeur. "You have bargained hard for it."

Lysander looked past him to the ledger crowded with human marks. "So I have."

* * *

The host did not leave as a shining river of steel. It departed in staged columns, because the first depot yard held only so many sleds and the Frostroad only so many hooves.

At six depots, keepers compared Sigrun's page with their own before releasing grain. Drivers changed cracked traces. Remount masters inspected fetlocks. Soldiers collected dry socks and tins of runner grease with the solemnity courtiers reserved for relics. When a sled axle split on the second day, pioneers lashed it to a spare and lost three hours. No mighty hand descended to return them.

Lysander rode beside Sigrun with the route ledger under his coat. He urged shorter rests until she pointed to horses blowing foam into the snow.

"They can sleep at Ninepin," he said.

"Dead horses are famous for resting," she said, and kept the halt.

On the third day, scouts found the river shelf cracked where the road curved east. Lysander knew a charcoal track along the ridge. It added seven miles but stayed on stone.

Sigrun did not take a prince's memory as a bridge. She sent two riders with measuring cord, questioned a depot keeper, and changed the route when their figures matched his.

The Redwater carts reached the day-four post because the courier had carried Lysander's orders south. They brought grain and too little fodder. For one sick instant he saw the whole compact ending in an empty manger.

Then he opened his household horse train. His six escorts dismounted. Northern harness went onto Redwater animals, and the soldiers walked beside the sleds.

Late on the fifth night, the columns descended toward Ninepin tired, fed, and still together. Ahead, lamps moved away from the three marsh villages in orderly lines. Evacuation carts. Sluice crews. The orders he had given before asking what his authority could buy.

* * *

Ninepin Causeway rose scarcely a man's height above Reedmarsh, a stone-backed road with black water on either side. Two culverts ran beneath its shoulders. North lay Redwater's capital. South, torchlight multiplied along the road until the Black Reed League seemed to have brought down a strip of the night.

Sigrun anchored wagons wheel to wheel across the firm center. Shield-spears stood behind them, bows on two low mounds, pioneers at the culvert gates, scouts forward among the reeds. Redwater's watch waited behind the line with poles and shovels.

The thaw had begun. Water ticked under thinning ice.

"Open the culverts now," Lysander said. "Soften the shoulders before their train arrives."

"Our last village carts are still south of the western cut. So are twelve scouts."

"If the engineers lay fascines first—"

"Then we move them. I will not bury our own people to improve the ground. Bring me the clearance report."

He nearly told her he was prince here. Instead he took four riders down the drainage path until they found the last carts grinding north, one wheel sunk to its hub. Lysander put his shoulder beside the villagers and the watch. By the time the wheel rose, Black Reed horns sounded across the marsh.

The report reached Sigrun as the first cavalry tested the reeds and found water under the crust. Six hundred horse narrowed into a useless, stamping column. Black Reed engineers came on foot, laying bound reeds over the soft shoulders while siege wagons advanced along the center.

Northern bows slowed them. They did not erase them. Shafts struck shields and men fell on both sides of the wagons. Spears met at the first barricade with a sound like timber dropped on stone. Healers worked in the lee of the mound. Drivers carried water forward and the injured back.

When the last scouts crossed, Sigrun lowered her arm. "West culvert. Half gate. Hold the east."

Pioneers turned the windlass. Marsh water spread across one shoulder in a dark, deliberate sheet. Black Reed's outer fascines shifted.

"East gate!" she called.

The second windlass would not move.

A watch member hammered its pin with a maul. "Jammed below!"

Lysander knew the maintenance cut from childhood inspections, a narrow ditch behind the stone lip. "Poles," he said. "Six with me."

The water reached his thighs before he found the gate's lower brace. Cold punched the breath from him. Watch members wedged poles under the timber while northern pioneers held the crumbling bank above them. On the road, another siege wagon struck the barricade.

"Together," Lysander said.

The first heave slipped. The second cracked something in his shoulder. On the third, the brace tore free and the east gate dropped open.

Water flung him against the stone lip. Hands dragged him onto the bank, bruised and coughing. Five watch members came after him.

They called twice for the sixth. No answer came from the brown rush beneath the culvert.

There was no time to make that absence noble. The eastern shoulder began to dissolve.

Two Black Reed siege wagons tilted into the softened verge. One went over, slow and enormous, its wheels blocking half the causeway. The next driver tried to turn and wedged his wagon across the remaining road. Sigrun advanced shield-spears far enough to secure the blockage, then stopped them. Fresh companies replaced the exhausted ones. Grain came forward. Dry socks came forward. The wounded went back on sleds that had not been burned for cook fires or lost to hungry foraging.

Black Reed probed for two days. Its horse could not deploy. Its foot could not bring numbers through the blocked center, and its engineers could not clear the wagons under the northern bows before the marsh swallowed each new shoulder path. With its supply train stretched south and the siege road closed, the League withdrew toward Greyglass.

Lysander watched the banners recede. Somewhere beyond them rode the marshal who had sold the gate.

"We pursue," he said. "Your scouts with my riders. We can take him before Greyglass."

"No border pursuit," Sigrun said. She did not lift the compact. She did not need to. "The causeway is held. My people have marched and fought for seven days."

Rank rose in Lysander's mouth out of habit, ready to turn need into command.

He swallowed it. "Send riders to observe the retreat. The rest help the villages home."

Sigrun gave the order. The northern host remained at Ninepin, exactly as far as it had promised to go.

* * *

Before the twentieth day, the first northern columns started home. Redwater's watch held the repaired barricade. Families returned to damp houses. Greyglass remained in enemy hands, but the siege train was broken and the capital granaries stood unopened.

The victory accounts were less handsome. Wages. Horses. Three burned roofs. Road stone. Injuries. Eleven northern dead. Four from Redwater, including the watch member the culvert had not returned. The seven-year toll fund had begun spending before anyone could praise it.

Lysander's tribunal was set for the first week after the thaw. His council had sent no hint of its succession decision. Sigrun would face the seven reeves in Harrowfast, and Gorm had not answered any of her dispatches.

At Ninepin, they signed the final tallies on a field table repaired with plain wooden braces.

"One remaining article," Lysander said.

Sigrun read it before signing. The marriage promise between Redwater and Gorm's house was void. No debt survived it. No northern service depended upon it.

She placed the severed gold clasp beside his hand. The chain itself had already been weighed and paid into the casualty fund.

"Keep it," he said.

"It was yours. The part that bought anything is gone."

He closed his fingers around the cold metal, then opened them again. Formal release language waited on his tongue, clean and useless.

"After the tribunal," he said, "may I write to you? Myself, I mean. Not through a king."

Sigrun checked the last toll figure. "You may write one letter."

"And after that?"

"I may answer it."

It was not a betrothal, forgiveness, or even a promise of a second page. It was enough because it was exactly what she had offered.

The last supply sled creaked north. Its runners left two modest grooves among hundreds of boot tracks. Lysander and Sigrun walked beside it on separate footing, while the unused clasp lay cold in his open palm.

stories.title: Four Million Falling
stories.prompt: In a fantasy world much like our own, where magic has long since die out, the greatest wonder is a floating city that should not be possible. With over four million residents, it's ancient nuclear reactors are beginning to fail, and the results are catastrophic.
stories.body:
# Four Million Falling

### 0:00

The cup moved three millimetres before the alarms began.

Inez Arco watched it creep across Chief Damas's console, leaving a crescent of coffee on the old black surface. Above it, the calibration weight hung at half a degree from vertical. Half a degree was nothing in a city that crossed weather fronts. Half a degree during a routine load-transfer test meant the floor and the world had stopped agreeing.

Then Reactor Four's board went red.

PRIMARY COOLANT PRESSURE LOW. SCRAM COMPLETE. TURBINE TRIP.

Inez was already out of her chair when the generator trace snapped flat. The isolation lamps changed from amber to green: commanded open. Current continued to pour across the common bus.

"Breaker Four is still closed," she said.

Damas caught his cup before it reached the edge. "Confirm."

"Four commanded open. No contact change. Bus current rising."

The control room lights dimmed. Somewhere below the consoles, a relay began hammering fast enough to blur into a buzz. Reactor One vanished from the generation display, then Five. Three and Six followed so closely their alarms arrived on top of each other. Reactor Two held for two more seconds.

The floor dropped.

Not far. Perhaps the thickness of Inez's hand before the lift rings caught the city's weight again. Her knees knew, though. Four million sets of knees would know. Loose binders lifted and slapped down. Someone behind her shouted once.

"Authorize a bus retry," Inez said. "If the breaker rail resets, I can bring a converter bank back before the rings coast."

"No." Damas's voice stayed level because that was part of his job. "Arco, prove ring integrity. Reactor desk, confirm all scrams. Cooling desk, emergency trains by unit."

"The bus is the source. Give me one reset."

"Prove the rings."

Procedure had become a wall, so she stopped pushing at it. Inez pulled the six generator phase traces across the lift board. Four's trace had not simply died. It had broken into a violent comb, an arc reaching through damaged insulation onto the bus. Each remaining generator had fed the same fault until its protection tripped the turbine and shut its reactor down. The isolation commands had gone out. The old shared actuator rail, bridged last winter when replacement parts failed inspection, had opened none of the breakers.

The ring diagram steadied under her hands: six concentric bands, all intact, all losing stored field energy.

"Rings are continuous," she said. "No converter input. We're coasting."

Damas looked at the vertical-rate estimate. It revised twice, settling as the stored fields weakened and Orison's fall accelerated.

TIME TO LETHAL CONTACT: 00:51:08.

### 0:08

The bus-gallery camera showed a white scar where the copper spine had been. Smoke folded through the image until the lens disappeared.

"No restart to save," Damas said. "Confirm."

Inez hated confirmation loops when the answer was obvious. She hated more that they were useful. "Confirmed. Main bus physically destroyed."

All six fission cores were shut down. Five had scrammed cleanly after the load rejection; Four had suffered a primary-coolant rupture, and emergency cooling on Two was cycling badly. None was exploding. None needed to. Their generators were gone, the lift converters were dark, and decay heat still had to be carried out of six ancient reactor blocks by pumps now competing for emergency power.

Orison's phones woke together. Inez's vibrated across the console with the civic alert.

**LIFT INTERRUPTION. SHELTER IN PLACE ABOVE BLUE DECK. DO NOT USE TRANSIT. AWAIT DISTRICT ROUTES.**

The population line beneath it read 4,083,612. A planning number, ordinarily. Water demand, school places, grain allotments. Now every digit had weight.

Reports crowded the side screens. Trains had braked in tunnels and platforms were filling faster than stairs could clear them. Three hospitals were on reserve power. The western shelter map showed twice its rated occupancy; eastern districts reported a southward slope, while the Low Keels reported north, because the city was flexing between rings. Fire crews needed priority lanes that no longer existed. Almost half a million people worked or lived below Blue Deck during the day. They had forty-three minutes to climb.

Inez opened the emergency generator diagram. "Cross-connect Unit Three's black-start set to Converter Two. Six minutes at full output buys us nine minutes of field."

"It buys the rings six at best," Damas said. "And leaves Three without a cooling train."

"Three scrammed clean."

"Three is still hot. Four has one cooling loop. Two's pump is hunting. The generators stay with cooling."

She threw the calculation onto his board: megajoules, field decay, vertical velocity. "At least look at the gain."

"I have. No lift recharge at the price of a damaged core."

The refusal left no softer version of the same request. Inez closed her model. Five intact reactors had done what their protections demanded, and the city was still falling. She made herself look at what remained rather than what she wanted to restart.

"Then tell me what stored field we still own."

Damas nodded once. The ring desk sent the numbers.

Inez ran them against current mass and contact speed. Then she ran them again with a lower final deceleration, enough to break windows and bones but not whole districts. The result did not improve.

"We can reach the sea alive," she said, "if we lose twelve percent of mass."

The Low Keels lit beneath the city diagram: freight vaults, reservoirs, sewage works, workshops, and stacked housing bolted below the oldest ring deck.

Paz's clinic occupied Keel South Three.

### 0:17

There was no time to call her yet. That was the first lie Inez told herself.

She built the landing from forces she could still command. Clear the Keels upward. Fire their separation charges. Bleed the inner rings in sequence to keep the city level as mass fell away. Hold the outer two rings until the last minutes, then spend their fields in one deceleration pulse against the world's magnetic field. The rings did not abolish gravity; they exchanged momentum while powered and held a finite charge when they were not. Once that charge was gone, there was no hidden reserve, ancient spell, or clever restart waiting beneath the numbers.

Damas studied her model. "Keep South Three. Drop the freight keels and the northern tanks."

"Not enough."

"Recalculate at fourteen metres per second contact."

"I did. South Three drags the southern edge down first. Ring Four saturates correcting it, then we roll before contact."

"Council authorization for inhabited separation requires projected loss comparison."

"The Council has twenty-nine minutes to learn field balance."

"Then give me something I can order without guessing."

His calm finally cracked on the last word. Not much, but enough. Inez set the two descent curves beside each other. In the version he wanted, southern housing remained attached for eleven minutes longer. Then the outer rings exhausted above the sea, Orison struck nose-low, and the reactor quarter went under first. The other curve ended in a city-wide injury estimate and a permanent ruin, but it ended below the fatal line.

"All Keels," she said. "Evacuation cutoff at thirty-four minutes. Separation immediately after."

"Confidence?"

"Enough to act. Not enough to forgive us."

Damas's gaze moved to the green actuator commands that had never opened anything. "Not now, Arco."

"My signature is on the bridge waiver. Individual breakers tested green. The common rail didn't. I said thirty more days was an acceptable exposure. If you're waiting for me to sound certain before you destroy those homes, this is why I sound certain."

For one second, neither of them performed calm.

Then Damas keyed the command channel. "All desks, prepare full Low Keel evacuation and separation. This is not a drill. Route every available stair upward. Suspend equipment security and open maintenance passages. Confirm by sector."

A voice from the emergency office asked whether the public notice should call the order a temporary clearance.

"No," Damas said. Procedure had failed him; euphemism did not survive it. "Call it emergency jettison. Tell them the Keels will be lost."

Inez's model began counting down to the first ring bleed.

### 0:25

The passage to the manual sequencer sloped enough that Inez had to use the handrail. People were coming the other way: technicians carrying battery lanterns, two orderlies supporting a man with a bandaged scalp, a reactor worker stripped to an undershirt and shaking from exertion. Nobody asked her whether the city would remain in the sky. The public alert had answered that.

At the stair landing, an old mosaic showed robed magicians dissolving into gold dust while workers raised Orison above them. Every schoolchild knew the caption: *When magic died, human hands built the greatest wonder.* Inez had once corrected Paz for calling the lift rings enchanted. They were measurable, she had said. As if wonder and measurement were enemies.

She called.

Paz answered on the fourth attempt. Behind her came shoes on metal stairs, wheels knocking each riser, and someone counting to three over and over.

"You're moving?" Inez asked.

"Forty-one patients, twelve staff, six neighbours who came in when the lifts stopped. Two beds won't fit the south stair turn. What's our cutoff?"

"Use maintenance stair K. It opens beside your pharmacy wall. Code six-zero-one."

There was a pause, filled by the sound of a bedframe striking metal.

"Who else has that route?" Paz asked.

"You do now."

"That's not what I asked."

"Paz, you're losing time."

"So are the dialysis ward and the nursery upstairs. Did you give them the code?"

Inez reached the sequencer door. Its battery lock was dead, and she had to shoulder it while entering the mechanical override. "The maintenance stair isn't rated for a public load."

"But it's rated for your sister."

The door gave. Inez stumbled into a low room where six manual ring controls curved around a window. The sea had risen visibly toward the city, blue and impossible beyond the glass.

"The Keels are being detached," she said. Reassurance was another form of theft now. "South Three too. I can hold separation until minute thirty-four. I cannot hold it longer."

Paz did not answer at once. The counting behind her stopped, then resumed farther away.

"How many stairs stay open if the deck tilts five degrees?"

"K and the central paired shafts. Avoid west crossways."

"When do the lights fail?"

"They already might. Your phones should keep the route map."

"Then broadcast K to the whole clinic block. Not just us."

Inez opened the emergency route channel and stripped the maintenance restriction from stair K. Occupancy estimates jumped at once: hundreds diverting, then thousands. Too many for comfort, within the structural limit if they did not run.

"Done," she said.

"Good. Hold us until the stairwell clears. Don't promise anything else."

"I will hold South Three until the stairwell clears."

"Last bed is moving now."

The connection broke before Inez could tell whether Paz had hung up or the network had.

### 0:35

The first Keel released cleanly. Its indicator vanished, and Orison rolled half a degree as thirty thousand tonnes fell away. Inez bled Ring Two east to correct.

The second release tore a freight bridge in half. Through the sequencer window, she saw a dark platform turn under the city, its cargo containers spilling in a slow glitter. It struck the Inner Sea seconds later. The impact rose as a white disk, then as sound through the city's bones.

Keels North One and South Two followed. Warning boards reported fires where utility lines had failed to sever. A shelter stair collapsed in a district Inez could not see. The casualty field remained blank because nobody had time to count.

South Three stayed yellow.

LATCH BANK C: CLOSED.

The evacuation desk transmitted overlapping fragments: central shafts clear above Blue Deck; stair K traffic still moving; smoke in the west crossway; clinic group unconfirmed.

"Delay separation," Inez said.

Damas answered through the command speaker. "Negative. Continue sequence."

"South Three has a mechanical hold. I need evacuation confirmation."

"Outer-ring reserve is falling faster than model. Release it."

"Paz's stair is in that sector."

"I know."

"Then give them another minute."

"No minute available. You have nineteen seconds before Ring Four exceeds correction capacity. At zero, keeping that Keel risks the remaining city."

She waited for the order. Damas did not give it.

"Your sequence," he said. "Your call."

The latch had no remote mechanical backup. The original builders might have known why; their diagrams ended at the housings, and every later generation had copied the gap. Inez could force current through the nearest inner-ring segment, far beyond its converter limit. The field pulse would wrench the attached structure downward and tear the latch out. It would also burn the segment open forever.

Twelve seconds.

She could hold the Keel and watch the southern mass overwhelm Ring Four. She could drop it with Paz somewhere inside. Another calculation would only spend seconds while pretending not to choose.

Inez armed the overload. "South Three destructive release. Ring Three segment south-six."

"Confirmed," Damas said.

She pressed both switches.

The current meter struck its stop. Heat pushed through the console into her palms. Outside, the skyline bent: towers, antennae, and the low roofs of a district that had always hung beneath her feet. A line of blue light flashed along the ring housing, electrical and brief. The stuck latch tore free.

South Three fell.

For an instant it remained level below Orison, streets and clinic windows small enough to cover with her hand. Then it tipped into the smoke from its severed utilities. Inez kept her hand on the dead switch until the indicator went black.

"Mass target achieved," Damas said. No triumph entered the words. "Begin landing sequence."

Inez spent the inner rings one at a time. Each bleed reduced their stored field and slowed the growth of vertical speed; each correction bought level at the cost of the final pulse. Orison groaned as loads found paths no designer had intended. The sea filled the window. Rescue vessels below scattered from the city's shadow, leaving white wakes that looked motionless at this height.

Ring Two's western switch froze halfway.

The city rolled. Cabinets burst open. A drawer crossed the floor and struck Inez's ankle. Instrument tilt said four degrees, then six, but its sensor had lost power and continued reporting six while the horizon climbed.

She stopped trusting it. The visible sea was level. Orison was not.

"Burn east-five," she said.

"That is our second permanent loss," Damas replied.

"If we don't, the outer rings spend themselves fighting roll."

"Approved."

She overloaded Ring Two's opposite segment. A bang sounded somewhere deep in the structure. The horizon slowed, held, then settled almost straight across the window.

At minute forty-six, outer-ring telemetry corrected itself.

Not enough reserve.

The field estimate had been borrowing a failed temperature sensor, reading the outer conductors colder and more efficient than they were. Inez had three minutes of gentle braking on paper and less than one in metal.

"We can stretch the pulse," Damas said. "Keep ten percent for contact and buoyancy support."

He had shifted to bargaining because command could not change the charge meters.

"A stretched pulse leaves us at twenty-one metres per second," Inez said. "The lower decks won't survive."

"No reserve means the city settles with full weight."

"The sealed ring trunks may float long enough for boats. They won't matter if impact splits them."

"Contact speed?"

She shortened the pulse window until the line crossed survivable. "Eleven, if the field holds."

The civic channel filled with shelter confirmations. Millions crouched in schools, offices, stations, and reinforced corridors. There was no room to move them now, only time to tell them what was coming.

Damas keyed the public line. "Brace. Final deceleration in thirty seconds. Impact will follow. Stay away from exterior walls."

Inez set both outer rings to discharge together. No field remained in the inner pair she had burned, and none would remain in the outer pair after this. Orison would never hover on these rings again.

Ten seconds. The sea lost detail until it became a single hard surface.

Five. She locked her elbows around the console rail.

At zero, she spent the wonder.

The field took hold through the floor, a pressure in her teeth and spine. Vertical speed fell. Displays died one by one as the battery bus collapsed under the switching load. The horizon stayed nearly level.

Then Orison hit the Inner Sea.

Water erased the window. The first impact drove Inez to her knees; the second threw her sideways as the city settled unevenly. Metal screamed below. Glass burst somewhere behind her. Cold water punched through the door seam, climbed to her wrists, and stopped.

For the first time in its remembered history, Orison was no longer falling.

### After

The control room canted seven degrees to the south. Inez knew because the battery inclinometer had revived, but she checked the horizon anyway.

The window was cracked and half above water. Smoke trailed from two lost districts. Steam rose from the reactor quarter where emergency cooling continued on local generators. Four's damaged loop still demanded work; a contamination boundary would have to be drawn across part of the sea. Below Blue Deck, water moved through streets built for rain but never tides.

Damas sat against a console while a medic wrapped his forearm. "You're finished here, Arco."

"Ring trunks?"

"Three flooded. Two holding. One uncertain. Boats are approaching from windward."

The first rescue craft could take hundreds. The next wave, thousands. Orison had held 4,083,612 residents that morning, plus visitors nobody had counted. Moving the survivors would take days if the weather stayed kind. Feeding them on a dead city would begin before that. None of them had a home that could rise again.

Inez tried to stand. Her left ankle refused her weight.

"Sit," Damas said.

"I can bring up the shelter ledger."

"No console. That's an order."

She almost argued that work was rest if the alternative was waiting. The lie had worn thin.

"Did the clinic stairwell clear?" she asked.

Damas looked toward the emergency desk. He did not soften his face before answering. "Partial receiving list came through Central School. Paz Arco arrived with thirty-seven patients and nine staff. Four patients and three staff from the clinic group are still unlocated. Other names are coming in."

Relief hurt differently from impact. It did not restore South Three. It did not fill the blank casualty fields or lift the freight workers whose platform had struck the sea first. It only gave Paz back to a world that now required somewhere else for her to live.

Outside, responders had stretched a rope along the tilted avenue. People passed water, bandages, and children hand to hand toward the rescue boats. Above them, the old school mosaic had broken along its caption. The golden magicians ended at the waterline; the workers raising Orison were gone beneath it.

No magic arrived to dispute the lesson. No dormant power lifted the city. The rings were burned and empty, the reactors shut down, and the sea kept what had fallen into it.

Inez took a place in the line. Her ankle shook each time she accepted a water tin, so the woman beside her shortened the distance without comment. Farther down, someone called for room for a stretcher, and the line opened, then closed again.

The horizon lay level at last. Against it, Orison rested crooked, terribly still.

stories.title: The Healer's Measure
stories.prompt: witchknights are not only master mages, but are also the most capable warriors. When one chose you to become their apprentice you were confused; You trained to be a healer. Apparently that's why they did.
stories.body:
# The Healer's Measure

Ruva saw the wrist before she saw the opening.

Vekran's practice blade was high, his right shoulder bare to a clean strike. That was the opening. The wrist beneath it was the truth: two tendons drawn tight under the skin, the thumb turned inward, one narrow line where a shallow cut would empty the hand without ruining it.

She went for the shoulder.

Three paces of sand vanished under her boots. Vekran did not retreat. He set the iron length of his blunted blade against hers, breathed out, and turned.

Pressure traveled through the blades like a kick from a mule. He had declared one turn before they began, and he spent it neatly. Ruva's own charge carried her past him. Her back foot crossed her front; the yard tipped; she landed hip-first in the sand.

Vekran stopped his blade a finger's width from her ribs.

"Halt."

Ruva lay still until the iron went away. The packed practice yard had been raked, its boundary checked, both blades inspected in her hands. Six weeks of bruises had taught her that Vekran meant every safety rule he gave her. They had not taught her how to fall without feeling personally insulted by the ground.

"Again," she said.

"What did you decline to strike?"

She sat up. "If you're looking for a graceful description of my failure, you'll have to recruit a poet."

"I recruited a healer."

There it was again: an answer shaped like a shut door. In every village along the road, children played at witchknights with broom handles. Soldiers lowered their voices over stories of warriors who could read a blow through iron and send it elsewhere. Vekran could have chosen any fighter who knew which end of a sword to hold. Instead he had walked into Ruva's treatment tent, watched her work for half a day, and offered her an apprenticeship she had spent six weeks proving she did not deserve.

He waited.

Ruva brushed sand from her sleeve. "Your wrist. Inside line. I could have stopped the hand without cutting the tendons if the blade were sharp."

"Yes. Next pass, that is your target."

"You want me to hesitate better?"

"I want you to reach the choice while someone is attacking you."

Hooves struck the road outside the yard. A rider pulled up hard enough to spray grit through the open gate. "The roadside infirmary. Medicine cart caught in an attack. The roof's going in."

Vekran was already exchanging the blunted blade for his edged one. "Ruva. Edged blade, warm cloak, healer's satchel."

She buckled on the edged apprentice blade and caught up the cloak and satchel from beside the fence. "All three?"

"All three."

The sword pulled at one hip. The satchel dragged at the other. She followed him through the gate with neither weight settled.

* * *

The medicine cart stood crooked across the infirmary courtyard, one wheel wedged against a stone trough. Bolts had punched through its canvas cover. A driver lay beside it with blood in their hair, and two attackers had the cart pinned from opposite sides while pressure groaned through the low building beyond.

Vekran touched the flat of his blade to the gatepost.

For one breath, nothing visible happened. Then his attention moved across the yard: roof, doorway, cart, hands. Ruva had learned enough of the measure to feel only a muddle through her own iron. He seemed to find every load at once.

A crossbow snapped.

Vekran stepped into the bolt. His blade met it at an angle too slight to stop anything. Breath and warmth moved from his living grip through the iron focus; the bolt changed course and buried itself in the empty water trough with a crack.

He was at the cart before the shooter had lowered the bow. An attacker cut for his neck. Vekran caught the sword close to its guard, bound it, and drove one shoulder into the wielder's chest. The same turn of his body put his free bracer under a lintel that tore loose above the driver. He sent the timber sideways into bare paving, twisted the sword from the attacker's hand, and kicked it under the cart.

One step, two threats, no wasted reach. This was why soldiers lowered their voices.

"Ruva. Take the driver. Rear route."

It sounded too much like stay out of the way.

She slid beside the driver anyway. "Can you hear me?"

The driver's eyes opened. Their pupils matched. Breathing quick, no wet rattle. The scalp wound bled freely but the skull beneath felt sound.

"I'm going to move you behind the wall. Press here. Hard." She put their hand over a folded cloth. "Ready?"

At their nod she pulled, keeping the neck straight, until the stone well curb lay between them and the crossbow.

The infirmary door bowed inward. Two walking patients stumbled into the yard, one supporting the other.

"Rear gate," Ruva called. "Stay low. Take the driver when you pass."

The crossbow attacker reached for another bolt. Vekran slapped his blade against the cart's iron rim, read the incoming pressure, and turned the next shot high over the wall. The magic took heat with it. His knuckles had gone pale. His next breath ended short.

The disarmed attacker rose behind him with a knife.

"Left rear," Ruva shouted.

Vekran pivoted before the knife reached him. He caught the wrist, folded it without breaking it, and sent the attacker face-down across the cart tongue. The crossbow shooter met him on the other side; Vekran slipped inside the stock, struck once with his sword guard, and caught the weapon before its owner hit the dust.

Ruva bound the driver's head, checked the two walking patients, and found a third person beneath the cart with a bruised leg but a strong foot pulse. She showed the mobile pair where to lift the axle, freed the trapped leg, and sent the driver and injured passenger through the rear gate. While Vekran stood between them and the fallen attackers, Ruva and the mobile pair rocked the wedged wheel clear of the trough. The axle cracked as they shoved the cart through the rear gate and left it behind the stone wall. The strip from the infirmary door past the trough stood empty. Three hurt. None bleeding to death. No red priority.

She drew her edged apprentice blade. "My route is clear. I'm coming to the door."

"Keep evacuating."

"You took me as an apprentice, not a porter with bandages."

The building groaned again. Dust streamed from the eaves.

Vekran looked at her then, not away from the doorway but somehow through the same attention. "You own the rear route until there are no red-priority patients. Report."

"None red. One head wound controlled. One leg injury, stable. Two mobile."

"Then advance under a shield-sized hold. No farther than you can retreat in three steps."

It was not reassurance. It was usable.

They crossed the threshold together. Inside, two patients crouched behind an overturned table. At the far roof post, a figure in a dark coat had one shoulder pressed against the wood and one hand clenched around an iron clasp fixed through torn clothing. Four lines of pressure ran from that point into the ceiling braces. The person held a knife in the other hand.

Vekran moved between the table and a falling beam. He planted his sword point in a crack between two floorstones, set his palm to the doorframe, and made a fixed brace from one surface to the other. The intact posts still carried most of the roof while the caster's working divided its pressure among four braces; Vekran took only the beam's sliding weight. It spent his warmth and fixed him at the doorway, but it was not yet the full crisis load. The beam stopped dropping. Timbers creaked around him.

The knife flashed from beside the post. Vekran shifted enough to keep it from his ribs, but the edge opened his sleeve under the upper arm.

He did not lose the ward. His jaw tightened once.

"Lane," he said.

Pressure gathered along Ruva's bracer, no wider than a shield. It gave her a path past the hanging beam.

She went in.

* * *

The knot-caster's knife had fallen after the strike. Ruva kicked it away before she knelt. Their skin had the gray cast of worsening shock, and the hand below the injured shoulder was darkening at the fingertips. Blood soaked the coat around the iron clasp, though not fast enough to explain the pulse Ruva could see jumping there.

It beat twice for every beat in the caster's throat.

"Don't touch it," they said. Their breath came shallow. "I let go, the roof comes down. Your witchknight cuts me, it comes down faster. So perhaps we discuss a door."

Behind Ruva, Vekran's partial brace hummed through stone and iron. "I can part the hard line through clasp and shoulder. I cannot map past it while I carry even this crossing load."

The fastest cut would end the living source. It would also cross muscle, vessels, perhaps the joint. Ruva looked at the four braces, each drawn toward the wounded shoulder as if the caster had tied the room to their own body and pulled.

"If I open a door," she said, "you can't walk to it. Your hand is losing blood. Your breath is failing."

"Then promise I leave alive."

"I can't promise freedom. I can examine the shoulder and press the wound, or I can stay back while he prepares the cut he can make. Those are the choices we have now."

The caster's mouth tightened. "A healer traveling with a witchknight. How comforting."

"Pressure, or no touch?"

The post creaked. One of the patients behind the table made a small sound.

"Pressure," the caster said. "The clasp stays."

Ruva set clean folded cloth around the iron, not over it. "I'm touching you now."

She pressed. The caster hissed and tried to turn away.

"Still. Or tell me to stop."

They held still.

Only then did Ruva give the healing working a little of her warmth. It passed through her palms, living attention following the gross boundaries beneath them: skin, torn muscle, the hard foreign edge of the clasp. She could encourage the small vessels to close and hold damaged edges where they belonged. She could not replace what had already been lost. She could not clean the wound while the iron remained, or give the caster back the heat shock had taken.

Cold climbed into her fingers.

The false pulse changed. Not a pulse at all. A second rhythm had been laid alongside the wound, tightening whenever the caster's breath stumbled. As Ruva held the tissue steadier, the pressure in the ceiling eased by a fraction.

Vekran felt it. "Again."

"I can't do more without spending what I'll need to move."

"Then don't. Name what changed."

Ruva followed the imposed rhythm as far as her touch allowed. It did not end at the clasp. It ran beside living tissue, borrowed the easiest path around the joint, then divided toward all four roof braces.

She took her hands away. "The working is braided along the wound. If you cut through the shoulder, all four loads release together."

The partial brace shuddered under Vekran's hand.

"My map was incomplete," he said at once. "I can keep the roof or attempt a second working. Not both."

No excuse. No performance of certainty. The partial brace was already cooling him. Taking all four roof lines would leave still less room for error.

Ruva pulled her cloak around the caster's uninjured side and looked for another line.

* * *

Blood had reached Vekran's cuff.

"Your arm first," Ruva said. "Thirty heartbeats and I can bind it."

"Assess it from there."

"You need stitches."

"First death?"

She hated the answer. "No. Painful. Steady loss, but the arm still bears weight. Your hand?"

"Cooling. Full feeling for now."

He had not dismissed her judgment. He had asked her to use it.

Ruva returned two fingers to the caster's shoulder. With the wound steadier, she could feel a narrow interval where the iron clasp touched the shaped pressure without crossing flesh. A finger's width at most. It shifted with each breath.

"There," she said. "Nonliving line. But it moves. I can't mark it once and trust it."

"Then you cut from the live map," Vekran said.

"I've parted chalk cord twice. Once cleanly."

"Name what you require."

"Someone qualified."

"Unavailable."

The caster gave a breath-short laugh that broke into a cough. "Your standards inspire confidence."

Ruva ignored them. Listing reasons had not changed the room. She changed tactics.

"A shield lane. A count I don't have to keep myself. Permission to abort if I lose the line."

"Yes. I drop the lane if my fingers go numb. If you lose the line, you stop. No blind cut."

"And the roof?"

"The posts carry most of it now, and the knot keeps its pressure divided. When you begin the final map, I take all four lines. About sixty heartbeats at full load."

The caster's hand closed over the clasp. "It stays. It's the only reason your people haven't killed me."

"It's also killing you," Ruva said. "Hold still and warn me when the false branch moves. I will try to separate it without cutting your shoulder. If you live, you go to treatment under ordinary guard. Not free. Alive."

"Try?"

"That's the true word."

The caster looked past her to Vekran. "And him?"

"Those are the terms," Vekran said. His voice had gone plain and thin. "Your companions have fled or fallen. Choose."

Dust spilled from a new crack overhead.

The caster released the clasp, though their fingers hovered beside it. "After each tightening, the false branch starts across on one. It lies over the living line on two and three. It clears on four. The gap after four lasts until the next tightening. I call every beat."

Ruva took chalk from her satchel and settled the edged apprentice blade in her grip. Stabilize for three breaths. Trace. Shift to guard. Turn the defensive pressure into bare floor. Part the braid. If the map blurred, stop.

Narrow enough to attempt. Too narrow for courage to improve.

* * *

Ruva tucked both hands into the warm fold of her cloak until her fingertips stung.

"Do I still have your yes to touch the shoulder?"

"Yes. The clasp stays until you cut it."

"If you pull away, I stop."

"This pass only settles the wound," Ruva told Vekran. "Keep the partial brace until I call the final map."

She cleaned the accessible skin, replaced the blood-wet cloth, and set her palms around the wound. Her warmth moved again. One breath: tissue edges, unsteady but distinct. Two: the caster's true pulse, quick beneath her little finger. Three: the imposed rhythm sliding beside it.

"Tightening," the caster whispered. "One."

Movement sounded at the broken side door.

An attacker from the courtyard lurched through, one hand braced on the frame, a short sword in the other. Their eyes found the caster.

"Traitor," they said, and drove forward.

Ruva released the healing working and stood. Six weeks had not taught her how to win a sword fight. Six weeks had taught her one short parry and how badly her guard recovered afterward.

The sword struck her bracer hard enough to bruise through leather. She caught it late, gave ground, and saw the attacker's wrist turn beneath the guard.

Inside line. The hand, not the shoulder.

Ruva cut once. The edge opened sleeve and skin shallowly across the exact disabling line. The attacker's grip sprang open. Their sword hit the floor.

She kicked it through the broken doorway. The attacker clutched the useless hand, stared at her, then stumbled after their fleeing companions rather than try Vekran's ward unarmed. Ruva did not pursue.

"Position," Vekran said.

Not praise. The thing she needed.

Ruva dropped beside the caster and raised a shield-sized hold as pressure snapped outward from the working they were still struggling to sustain. Her back foot slid in blood-damp dust. The hold buckled, flinging strain into her shoulder.

She let it go.

The pressure struck the wall above them and showered grit. Forcing the hold would have thrown it through the patients—or through Ruva.

"New count," she said. Her breath shook. "I lost the footing."

She shifted half a pace to dry stone. Her arm throbbed where the bracer had taken the sword. Vekran's hands shook now, too, but his partial brace remained fixed.

"Still yes?"

"Yes. Hurry."

"Call the branch. Nothing else."

The caster swallowed and nodded.

"The full load starts with my first breath," Ruva said.

"Ready," Vekran said.

Ruva put her palms back to the wound. Vekran drove his sword point deeper and, with one long exhale, interposed his fixed ward across all four roof lines. The ceiling settled the width of a finger as the intact posts shed their strain into him. His next breath stopped short.

"Full load," he said. "Sixty."

"First breath," Vekran counted.

Ruva found the living pulse.

"Second."

She found the false rhythm alongside it.

"Third breath. Forty-six heartbeats."

She drew chalk across the clasp where the narrow gap lay at that instant. Then she released the healing hold. The wound stayed bound by cloth and its own encouraged clotting, not cured, not safe for long.

Ruva shifted to guard.

The caster's trained reflex tightened the working as pain caught their breath. Pressure lashed from the clasp toward Ruva's chest. She met one bounded line with her bracer, set her weight through the dry back foot, and turned.

Force hammered into the floor. Tile split with a flat crack. Numbness rushed from her wrist to her elbow.

Moved, not erased.

"Thirty-four," Vekran said.

"One—moving," the caster gasped.

Ruva began the stroke toward the chalk mark, intending to land before the second beat.

"Two. Across. Stop."

The false branch slid across the living pulse.

Vekran's breath hitched. The beam above him dropped the width of a nail before his ward caught it again.

Every urgent part of Ruva wanted to finish the stroke. Faster. Stronger. Before the room chose for them.

But there was no safe line beneath her blade.

She aborted, drew back, and waited.

"Twenty-eight," Vekran said.

"Three. Hold," the caster said. Their whole body strained against the need to move. "Four. Clear. Now."

The false branch passed beyond the living pulse. In the promised gap before the next tightening, healer-sense gave Ruva the boundary her eyes could not: warm living tissue here, cold clasp there, shaped pressure crossing only the iron.

She cut on that line.

The blade passed through the edge of the clasp and the braided working with a sound like cloth tearing under water. The caster cried out but the edge cleared their shoulder.

The four roof loads released unevenly.

"Eighteen," Vekran said. He pulled his sword from the floor and turned with his whole body. He opened the ward toward the cleared strip between the doorway and the trough. Timber, tile, and force went outward through the path he chose, bursting across the empty paving in a roar of dust.

Then he dropped the hold before it could take the last warmth from his hands.

Part of the roof fell across the cleared strip, stopping short of the cart behind the rear wall. The inner beam settled onto the overturned table instead of the people behind it.

Vekran sank to one knee, conscious, his sword point resting on stone.

Ruva did not check whether anyone had seen her cut. She put the blade down, caught the caster before they slumped against the post, and pressed fresh cloth to the shoulder.

"Stay with me," she said. "The spell is over. The wound isn't."

* * *

By the time guards arrived from the road, Ruva had found six injuries, none immediately fatal. The driver needed watching for confusion. The patient with the bruised leg needed a splint for the journey. The caster needed warmth, fluids if they could keep them down, and proper cleaning before anyone considered removing what remained of the clasp.

Vekran needed stitches.

"Cloak first," Ruva told him.

"The caster—"

"Has mine and two warmed bricks. Give me your arm."

He did. His cut was shallow but longer than she had hoped, and his skin had the waxy chill of spent measurework. She cleaned and bound it; stitching could wait until there was better light and a roof that did not shed dust into open wounds.

The caster watched from a litter while a guard secured their uninjured wrist. Ruva checked the restraint for circulation, then checked the shoulder binding again.

"This isn't pardon," the caster said.

"No. It's transport. Keep that hand still."

They looked as if they had another taunt available. Exhaustion won. The litter went toward the road under guard.

The infirmary had lost half its roof. The medicine cart had a split axle and three bolts through its canvas. Those who could walk gathered blankets and unbroken jars from the dust. There would be repairs, statements, custody, more treatment. Nothing Ruva had done made those costs vanish.

Vekran sat against the wall with his bandaged arm inside the cloak. "Assessment."

Ruva was too tired to pretend not to know what he meant. "Of me?"

"By you."

She wanted one word: worthy or mistaken. He had never offered comfort where evidence would do, so she gave him the evidence.

"My recovery is weak. I failed the first hold because I didn't clear my footing. The turn worked and numbed my arm. The parting worked because the caster corrected my timing. I stabilized two patients." She looked at his bandage. "And one mentor who still needs stitches."

"Accurate."

"Is that why you chose me? To keep a witchknight alive after the work?"

"Partly. Not chiefly." He flexed his fingers, stopped when they trembled, and put the hand back under the cloak. "Anyone can be taught where to cut. I needed an apprentice already trained to ask what has to live through it."

Ruva glanced at the ruined room. "Then you should have said you wanted a healer. Not someone you meant to turn into a former healer."

"I thought bringing the satchel made that plain."

"It did not."

He considered this with the same seriousness he gave a bad map. "My error."

"The satchel stays in every field kit. Healing shifts count as witchknight training, not time away from it. Those are my terms."

"Agreed."

No ceremony. Ruva found that she preferred it.

Vekran nodded toward the broken tile where her turn had landed. "Your back foot was late."

"I noticed."

"Tomorrow—"

"Tomorrow you sleep. The day after, perhaps you may criticize my feet."

His mouth moved at one corner, too tired to become a smile.

When the damaged medicine cart finally rolled toward town, Ruva walked beside the patients. Her healer's satchel crossed one shoulder. Her edged apprentice sword crossed the other, cleaned and returned to its sheath.

The two weights pulled differently. After a dozen steps, Ruva stopped and shortened the sword strap until they balanced. Then she walked on.

stories.title: Hello, Lover
stories.prompt: A demon appears before your party, exclaiming “Hello lover!” Everyone looks at the bard, but then the cleric speaks up. “Actually, my ex is referring to me.”
stories.body:
# Hello, Lover

Emet Sarn had one hand on the stolen brass when he recognized the file mark.

Three shallow strokes crossed the lower hinge leaf, the middle one wandering crooked because Lacrixa had laughed into his shoulder while he worked. He had once known that scratch by touch in the dark. Now the leaf was bolted into an iron scaffold in a ruined roadside sanctuary, between three black loops and jars of salt-glass cloudy with someone else's stored charge.

“Familiar workmanship?” Udren asked from beneath the cracked arch. Her shield was already angled toward the doorway, the road settlement downhill, and every person who had ignored their warning to stay indoors.

Emet removed his thumb from the scratches. “Familiar principles.”

Not a lie, if one filed truth as badly as brass.

Bosk, the party's bard, crouched beside him, keeping his embroidered sleeves clear of the iron. “Can you quiet it?”

Emet pressed the stamped medallion at his throat, not for help from the inert silver but for the shelter-count cut into it. Breath in. Heat gathered behind his sternum. On the exhale, he fed a thread of his own ward-light through the stolen leaf to feel for the trap's edge.

The scaffold took everything he offered.

Heat drew an upright line in the air. The line opened hand-wide, showing red tile, white glare, and one amber eye.

Emet stopped breathing.

The opening widened. Lacrixa stepped through in a scorched traveling coat, a living demon from the far Cauterized Reach, one horn wrapped in a strip of copper cloth and her boot soles smoking against the sanctuary floor. She looked straight past Bosk and smiled at Emet with all her teeth.

“Hello lover!”

Everyone looked at Bosk.
